Lindera Documentation

Lindera

A morphological analysis library in Rust. Lindera is forked from kuromoji-rs and aims to provide easy installation and concise APIs for tokenizing text in multiple languages.

Key Features

FeatureDescription
Morphological AnalysisViterbi-based segmentation and part-of-speech tagging
Multi-language SupportJapanese (IPADIC, IPADIC NEologd, UniDic), Korean (ko-dic), Chinese (CC-CEDICT, Jieba)
Dictionary SystemPre-built dictionaries, user dictionaries, and custom dictionary training
Text Processing PipelineComposable character filters and token filters for flexible text normalization
CRF TrainingTrain custom CRF models for dictionary cost estimation
Python BindingsUse Lindera from Python via PyO3
WebAssemblyRun Lindera in the browser via wasm-bindgen
Pure RustNo C/C++ dependencies; works on any platform Rust supports

Tokenization Flow

graph LR
    subgraph Your Application
        T["Text"]
    end
    subgraph Lindera
        CF["Character Filters"]
        SEG["Segmenter\n(Dictionary + Viterbi)"]
        TF["Token Filters"]
    end
    T --> CF --> SEG --> TF --> R["Tokens"]

Performance

Lindera tokenizes Japanese text (IPADIC) at roughly 10-20 MB/s single-threaded, depending on hardware and whether the Viterbi lattice is reused across calls. Run make bench to reproduce the benchmark suite (lindera/benches/) on your own machine; see #875 for detailed methodology and comparison numbers.

Quick Example

use lindera::dictionary::load_dictionary;
use lindera::mode::Mode;
use lindera::segmenter::Segmenter;
use lindera::analysis::tokenizer::Tokenizer;
use lindera::LinderaResult;

fn main() -> LinderaResult<()> {
    let dictionary = load_dictionary("embedded://ipadic")?;
    let segmenter = Segmenter::new(Mode::Normal, dictionary, None);
    let tokenizer = Tokenizer::new(segmenter);

    let text = "関西国際空港限定トートバッグ";
    let mut tokens = tokenizer.tokenize(text)?;
    println!("text:\t{}", text);
    for token in tokens.iter_mut() {
        let details = token.details().join(",");
        println!("token:\t{}\t{}", token.surface.as_ref(), details);
    }

    Ok(())
}

Run the example:

cargo run -p lindera-analysis --features=embed-ipadic --example=tokenize

Output:

text:   関西国際空港限定トートバッグ
token:  関西国際空港    名詞,固有名詞,組織,*,*,*,関西国際空港,カンサイコクサイクウコウ,カンサイコクサイクーコー
token:  限定    名詞,サ変接続,*,*,*,*,限定,ゲンテイ,ゲンテイ
token:  トートバッグ    名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,*,*,*

Crate Overview

CrateTypeDescription
lindera-crfCorePure Rust CRF (Conditional Random Field) implementation. Supports no_std. Uses rkyv for serialization. Its console feature, without the training, writes to the standard streams without panicking; lindera-analysis and lindera-cli use it for their own messages.
lindera-dictionaryCoreDictionary base library. Provides dictionary loading and building.
lindera-trainerCoreCRF-based dictionary training pipeline. Builds on lindera-crf and lindera-dictionary; consumed directly or via the lindera facade's train feature.
lindera-segmenterCorePure morphological segmenter (the lindera crate of v6 and earlier). Integrates the dictionary crates and provides the Segmenter API.
lindera-analysisCoreLucene-style analysis chain on top of lindera-segmenter: character filters, token filters, and the Tokenizer that composes them around a Segmenter. Reachable as lindera::analysis.
linderaCoreFacade crate and the one dependency Rust users add: re-exports lindera-segmenter and, with the default analysis feature, lindera-analysis as lindera::analysis.
lindera-cliApplicationCommand-line interface for tokenization, dictionary building, and CRF training.
lindera-bindingCoreFFI-independent helpers shared by the five language bindings below; depends on the lindera facade.
lindera-dependencyCoreJapanese bunsetsu dependency analysis, published from 7.1.0 on: the core types, the lattice format of CaboCha, the schema of a dictionary with the head and the function word of a bunsetsu, the segmentation into bunsetsu (chunking), and a command that makes training data, trains the chunker and evaluates. Its default build depends on no other crate of the workspace. See Lindera Dependency.
lindera-ipadicDictionaryJapanese dictionary based on IPADIC.
lindera-ipadic-neologdDictionaryJapanese dictionary based on IPADIC NEologd (includes neologisms).
lindera-unidicDictionaryJapanese dictionary based on UniDic.
lindera-unidic-cwjDictionaryJapanese dictionary based on UniDic for contemporary written Japanese (UniDic CWJ).
lindera-unidic-csjDictionaryJapanese dictionary based on UniDic for contemporary spoken Japanese (UniDic CSJ).
lindera-sudachidictDictionaryJapanese dictionary based on SudachiDict.
lindera-ko-dicDictionaryKorean dictionary based on ko-dic.
lindera-cc-cedictDictionaryChinese dictionary based on CC-CEDICT.
lindera-jiebaDictionaryChinese dictionary based on Jieba.
lindera-pythonBindingPython bindings via PyO3.
lindera-nodejsBindingNode.js bindings via NAPI-RS.
lindera-rubyBindingRuby bindings via Magnus + rb-sys.
lindera-phpBindingPHP bindings via ext-php-rs.

Tokenization Pipeline

Lindera processes text through a multi-stage pipeline:

Input Text
  |
  v
Character Filters    -- Normalize characters (e.g., Unicode normalization, mapping)
  |
  v
Segmenter            -- Segment text into tokens using a dictionary and the Viterbi algorithm
  |
  v
Token Filters        -- Transform tokens (e.g., POS filtering, stop words, stemming)
  |
  v
Output Tokens

The Segmenter is the core component. It builds a lattice of candidate tokens from the dictionary, then applies the Viterbi algorithm to find the lowest-cost path, producing the most likely segmentation. Dictionary lookups walk a char-wise double-array trie (built with crawdad) in place over the serialized bytes of dict.trie, rather than deserializing into an owned structure. For repeated tokenization, Segmenter::new_worker() returns a SegmentWorker that reuses lattice and scratch-buffer allocations across calls, with an automatic shrink policy to bound retained memory.

Getting Started

This section will guide you through installing Lindera and running your first morphological analysis.

  • Installation -- Add Lindera to your project and set up a dictionary
  • Environment Variables -- The environment variables that Lindera, its CLI and the Ruby gem read
  • Quick Start -- Tokenize your first text in just a few lines of code

Installation

Requirements

Rust 1.89 or newer. The workspace declares this as rust-version, so an older toolchain reports it as a cargo error rather than failing to compile.

Adding the Dependency

Put the following in Cargo.toml:

[dependencies]
lindera = "7"

[!NOTE] This single dependency also provides the analysis chain (character filters, token filters, and the Tokenizer) as lindera::analysis; use default-features = false if you only need the segmenter. Upgrading from v6? See Migration v6 to v7 for details.

Dictionary Setup

Lindera requires a pre-built dictionary at runtime. Download a dictionary from GitHub Releases and specify its path when loading:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let dictionary = load_dictionary("/path/to/ipadic")?;
}

[!TIP] If you want to embed a dictionary directly into the binary (advanced usage), enable the corresponding embed-* feature flag and load it using the embedded:// scheme:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// Cargo.toml: lindera = { version = "7", features = ["embed-ipadic"] }
let dictionary = load_dictionary("embedded://ipadic")?;
}

An embed-* build of a dictionary crate from crates.io downloads the dictionary that its Lindera release put on GitHub, checks its SHA-256, and embeds it; it no longer builds the dictionary from source, so it needs access to github.com (which serves the file from release-assets.githubusercontent.com) rather than lindera.dev. A build from a checkout of the repository builds the dictionaries from source. With LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_CACHE_DIR, a later build uses the downloaded dictionary without network access. See LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_FROM_SOURCE for when the build script builds from source instead, and LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_PUBLISHED_BASE_URL for downloading from a mirror.

Only the bundled dictionaries can be embedded. Build your own dictionary with lindera build and load it from its directory at runtime.

See Feature Flags for details.

Environment Variables

The build scripts of the dictionary crates read LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_CACHE_DIR, LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_FROM_SOURCE, LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_PUBLISHED_BASE_URL, LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_SOURCE_BASE_URL, LINDERA_BUILD_CONTEXT_ID_FREQ_FILE and DOCS_RS, and TokenizerBuilder::new() reads LINDERA_CONFIG_FILE. See Environment Variables for these and the other variables that Lindera reads.

Environment Variables

Lindera reads the environment variables below; none of them is required.

VariableRead byValueWithout it
LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_CACHE_DIRThe build scripts of the dictionary cratesA directoryEach build downloads and builds the dictionary in its own output directory
LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_FROM_SOURCEThe build scripts of the dictionary crates1 or trueA dictionary crate downloads the published dictionary it pins, and builds from source only when it cannot use it
LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_PUBLISHED_BASE_URLThe build scripts of the dictionary cratesAn http or https URLThe published dictionaries are downloaded from GitHub releases
LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_SOURCE_BASE_URLThe build scripts of the dictionary cratesAn http or https URLThe source archives are downloaded from https://lindera.dev, UniDic's, UniDic CWJ's and UniDic CSJ's from NINJAL (https://clrd.ninjal.ac.jp), and ko-dic's from mecab-ko-dic's Bitbucket Downloads (https://bitbucket.org)
LINDERA_BUILD_CONTEXT_ID_FREQ_FILEThe build scripts of the dictionary cratesA fileThe histogram bundled with the dictionary crate, if any
LINDERA_BUILD_DEPENDENCY_MODEL_IPADIC_FILEThe build script of lindera-dependency, with embed-model-ipadic; ..._UNIDIC_FILE, ..._UNIDIC_CWJ_FILE and ..._UNIDIC_CSJ_FILE with the features of the models for UniDicA model fileA published crate embeds the model it pins; a build from the repository stops

Three of them have a former name that still works until v8.0.0, with a deprecation warning: LINDERA_CTX_FREQ_FILE for LINDERA_BUILD_CONTEXT_ID_FREQ_FILE, LINDERA_CONFIG_PATH for LINDERA_CONFIG_FILE, and LINDERA_DATA_DIR, read as LINDERA_DICTIONARIES_DIR=<dir>/dictionaries. See Migration v6 to v7.

Build-time variables

The build scripts of the dictionary crates, such as lindera-ipadic, read these variables when they build a dictionary, for example for lindera with an embed-* feature. They have no effect at runtime.

LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_CACHE_DIR

The LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_CACHE_DIR environment variable designates a build-time cache directory for the embedded-dictionary build pipeline. It is read only by the dictionary crates' build scripts and has no effect at runtime.

When set, each build stores two kinds of files under $LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_CACHE_DIR/<version>-fmt<format>/ (where <version> is the dictionary crate version and <format> is the dictionary format version):

  • the downloaded distribution archive (validated against the SHA-256 that the crate's build.rs pins; invalid files are re-downloaded)
  • the built binary dictionary, with a build_inputs.json that records what it was built from

The format version is part of the path so that a cache written by a build with a different on-disk dictionary layout is a miss rather than a stale hit. A cached dictionary is reused only when all of the following match the current build, and is rebuilt otherwise:

  • the dictionary format version and the contents of the crate's metadata.json
  • the lindera-dictionary crate that builds it: its version and a digest of its source, so that any change to the dictionary builder, an uncommitted one included, rebuilds the dictionary
  • the source archive (file name and SHA-256) and the directory the build reads in it
  • the context-id frequency histogram the build reads (context_id_freq.txt, or the file named by LINDERA_BUILD_CONTEXT_ID_FREQ_FILE) when connection_id_mapping is enabled

A published dictionary that a build downloads instead of building it (see LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_FROM_SOURCE) is cached in the same place, and build_inputs.json records it by its key and SHA-256 besides the inputs above. The next build that would download the same published dictionary uses the cached one; a build that switches between the published dictionary and the build from source replaces it.

A dictionary left behind by an interrupted build, or cached by a release from before build_inputs.json, is rebuilt. The versions of the builder's dependencies are not compared: after upgrading a dependency of lindera-dictionary without a format version change, clear the cache if the built dictionaries may differ. Directories from older format versions are not deleted automatically; remove them by hand if the cache grows.

A build does not embed the cached files themselves: it links the nine files of the dictionary into the build script's output directory (OUT_DIR), copies those it cannot link (when the cache is on another file system than the target directory, for example), and embeds them from there. A crate thus keeps the dictionary it embedded when another build, with other inputs, replaces the cached one, or when the cache is removed, and builds in any checkouts and target directories can share one directory.

cargo build -vv shows, for each dictionary crate, whether the cached dictionary was used and why or why not, and whether it was linked or copied, on lines that start with lindera dictionary cache:.

This enables:

  • Offline builds: once cached, subsequent builds need no network access
  • Faster builds: download and dictionary build are skipped when valid cached files exist
  • Reproducible builds: consistent dictionary versions across builds

Usage:

export LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_CACHE_DIR=/path/to/cache
cargo build --features=embed-ipadic

To share one directory among every target directory and worktree, set an absolute path once: in the shell profile, as above, or in ~/.cargo/config.toml, which cargo passes to the build scripts:

[env]
LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_CACHE_DIR = "/path/to/cache"

Changing the value under [env] reruns the build scripts, as changing the variable does, and a variable set in the shell takes precedence over [env].

Notes:

  • The directory is managed automatically and is safe to delete: a crate already built keeps the dictionary it linked or copied, and the next build that needs a dictionary downloads or builds it again
  • Version subdirectories accumulate across upgrades and are not garbage-collected; old ones can be removed freely
  • Setting this variable causes dictionary crates to download and build their dictionaries even when no embed-* feature is enabled (useful for pre-populating the cache). Such a build embeds nothing, so it keeps a dictionary already in the cache without checking it; a build with the embed-* feature checks it and rebuilds it if needed
  • A relative path resolves under the workspace root, which, in this repository, gives each checkout its own cache; set an absolute path to share one
  • Checkouts whose builders differ, or whose builds differ in their inputs (LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_FROM_SOURCE, for example), replace each other's cached dictionaries when their build scripts run, which costs a download or a build each time, but does not change what an already built crate embeds
  • A cache kept between CI runs, for example with actions/cache, needs a key that changes with Cargo.lock as well as with lindera-dictionary and the dictionary crate, since the versions of the builder's dependencies are not compared. This repository's CI keeps one entry per dictionary under such a key (.github/actions/dictionary-cache)
  • Builds that share the directory, such as cargo build alongside rust-analyzer with its own target directory, write each dictionary one at a time: a build that finds another build writing the same dictionary waits for it, and then uses the dictionary it left (cargo build -vv shows lindera dictionary cache: waiting for another build). The lock is an empty <dictionary>.lock file next to the dictionary, held while a build writes it. It works between builds on one machine, and on a network file system only as far as the file system supports file locks. Where the file cannot be locked, the build prints a warning and goes on without the lock, as builds before 7.0.0 did, so two such builds can still remove each other's files
  • Builds with DOCS_RS set ignore this variable (see DOCS_RS below)

LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_FROM_SOURCE

A Lindera release builds the nine official dictionaries from source and puts them on the page of its version, next to the binaries, as lindera-<name>-<version>.zip. A dictionary crate published on crates.io pins its release's archive, by URL and SHA-256, in the prebuilt.json next to its metadata.json, which the release writes, and its build script downloads that archive, checks it, and embeds it, instead of downloading the source archive and building the dictionary. The archive holds the same files as a build from source; only the lindera_version in its metadata.json names the release. How the dictionaries are published is in Dictionary Release.

A failed download, an archive with another SHA-256, or one that lacks a file or does not fit the crate's metadata.json, stops the build with an error that says what went wrong; the build does not embed anything it could not check, and does not build from source instead.

The build script builds the dictionary from source, as up to v6, in these cases:

  • LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_FROM_SOURCE is 1 or true. 0, false and the empty value leave the choice to the build script; any other value counts as 1, with a warning.
  • LINDERA_BUILD_CONTEXT_ID_FREQ_FILE names a histogram, with which the dictionary differs from the published one.
  • The pinned dictionary has another dictionary format version than this build reads, which a pin that a release writes never has.
  • The crate has no prebuilt.json, as when it is built from this repository (a checkout or a git dependency) rather than from crates.io.

In the first three cases, the build script says why in a warning, such as:

warning: lindera-ipadic@7.0.0: building the ipadic dictionary from source, because LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_FROM_SOURCE is set

Cargo shows these warnings for a dictionary crate built from a path, such as a checkout of this repository; for one from crates.io, it shows them only when the build fails or runs with cargo build -vv. Changing the variable, or prebuilt.json, reruns the build script. Builds with DOCS_RS set build neither: they use dummy dictionaries (see DOCS_RS below).

LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_FROM_SOURCE=1 cargo build --features=embed-ipadic

LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_PUBLISHED_BASE_URL

LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_PUBLISHED_BASE_URL and LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_SOURCE_BASE_URL point the downloads of the build scripts at mirrors, for builds that must not reach the hosts Lindera publishes on, such as builds that go through a proxy repository like Artifactory. Each variable replaces one host:

VariableReplacesThe build downloads
LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_PUBLISHED_BASE_URLhttps://github.com/lindera/lindera/releases/download, the base_url in the crate's prebuilt.json<base>/<path>, with the path in prebuilt.json
LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_SOURCE_BASE_URLhttps://lindera.dev, where the crate's build.rs downloads the source archive from; for UniDic, NINJAL's https://clrd.ninjal.ac.jp/unidic_archive/cwj/2.1.2, for UniDic CWJ and UniDic CSJ, NINJAL's https://clrd.ninjal.ac.jp/unidic_archive/2512, and for ko-dic, mecab-ko-dic's Bitbucket Downloads, https://bitbucket.org/eunjeon/mecab-ko-dic/downloads<base>/<file_name>, with the archive's file name

For IPADIC, with the variables set to https://mirror.example/lindera-releases and https://mirror.example/lindera-dev, the build downloads one of these:

https://mirror.example/lindera-releases/v7.0.0/lindera-ipadic-7.0.0.zip
https://mirror.example/lindera-dev/mecab-ipadic-2.7.0-20250920.tar.gz

A mirror thus keeps the files at the paths they have on the original host: an Artifactory remote repository that proxies https://github.com/lindera/lindera/releases/download serves the published dictionaries, and one that proxies https://lindera.dev serves the source archives. The source archives of UniDic, UniDic CWJ, UniDic CSJ and ko-dic do not come from lindera.dev: a mirror that builds them from source serves NINJAL's unidic-mecab-2.1.2_src.zip, unidic-cwj-202512_full.zip and unidic-csj-202512_full.zip, and Bitbucket's mecab-ko-dic-2.1.1-20180720.tar.gz, at the same base, under those file names. lindera.dev has a mecab-ko-dic-2.1.1-20180720.tar.gz too, the one v6 builds from: it holds the same release repacked but fails the SHA-256 check, so the mirror serves Bitbucket's in its place. A build downloads the published dictionary by default and the source archive only when it builds from source (see LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_FROM_SOURCE), which can also happen without LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_FROM_SOURCE; a build that must not reach the original hosts sets both variables.

export LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_PUBLISHED_BASE_URL=https://mirror.example/lindera-releases
export LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_SOURCE_BASE_URL=https://mirror.example/lindera-dev
cargo build --features=embed-ipadic
  • The mirror replaces the host: the build downloads from the mirror alone, and never from the original host, even when the mirror fails.
  • The build checks what it downloads against the SHA-256 that the dictionary crate pins, as it does for the original host, and a mirror that serves another file stops the build.
  • The value is an http or https URL; a trailing / is ignored. The build sends no credentials, so the mirror has to serve the files without authentication. A URL with a user name or a password is an error, as is one with a query or a fragment, which the build could not append the path to. An empty value means no mirror.
  • The cache of LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_CACHE_DIR keeps a dictionary and a source archive by their SHA-256, not by the host they came from, so a build with a mirror uses what a build without one cached, and the other way round.
  • Changing either variable does not rerun the build script, since the dictionary is the same from any host. A build script that failed, for example because it could not reach the original host, runs again on the next build.
  • Only the build scripts read the variables. lindera download downloads its dictionaries from GitHub at run time.

LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_SOURCE_BASE_URL

The mirror of the dictionary source archives, which the build downloads as <base>/<file_name> in place of https://lindera.dev/<file_name> (for UniDic, UniDic CWJ and UniDic CSJ, in place of NINJAL's URL, and for ko-dic, in place of Bitbucket's). See LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_PUBLISHED_BASE_URL, which describes both variables.

LINDERA_BUILD_CONTEXT_ID_FREQ_FILE

The LINDERA_BUILD_CONTEXT_ID_FREQ_FILE environment variable names a context-ID frequency histogram that the dictionary crates' build scripts read in place of the context_id_freq.txt bundled with the crate. It applies only to a dictionary whose metadata.json enables connection_id_mapping, as those of UniDic, UniDic CWJ, UniDic CSJ and ko-dic do among the bundled dictionaries, and has no effect at runtime. The histogram orders the context IDs of the connection cost matrix so that frequent ones sit close together, which changes the speed of tokenization but never its result; the ctxfreq_dump example of the lindera crate writes one from a corpus.

export LINDERA_BUILD_CONTEXT_ID_FREQ_FILE=/path/to/context_id_freq.txt
cargo build --features=embed-unidic

Only the build scripts read it: lindera build takes the histogram from its --context-id-freq option, and the functions of the bindings that build a dictionary take it as an optional argument, context_id_freq (contextIdFreq in Node.js). Changing the variable, or the file it names, reruns the build script, and the cache of LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_CACHE_DIR compares the histogram's contents. With the variable set, the build script builds the dictionary from source rather than downloading the published one (see LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_FROM_SOURCE).

LINDERA_CTX_FREQ_FILE, the name of this variable up to v6, still works until v8.0.0, with a deprecation warning:

warning: lindera-ko-dic@7.0.0: LINDERA_CTX_FREQ_FILE is deprecated and will be removed in v8.0.0; set LINDERA_BUILD_CONTEXT_ID_FREQ_FILE instead

When both are set, LINDERA_BUILD_CONTEXT_ID_FREQ_FILE is used, and the warning says that LINDERA_CTX_FREQ_FILE is ignored. Cargo shows these warnings for a dictionary crate built from a path, such as a checkout of this repository; for one from crates.io, it shows them only when the build fails or runs with cargo build -vv.

LINDERA_BUILD_DEPENDENCY_MODEL_IPADIC_FILE

LINDERA_BUILD_DEPENDENCY_MODEL_IPADIC_FILE names the model file that a build with embed-model-ipadic (embed-dependency-ipadic in lindera, its command and the bindings) embeds: the model of lindera-dependency for IPADIC.

Each model for UniDic has a variable of its own, read the same way by the build with its feature:

VariableFeature of lindera-dependencyModel
LINDERA_BUILD_DEPENDENCY_MODEL_UNIDIC_FILEembed-model-unidicunidic
LINDERA_BUILD_DEPENDENCY_MODEL_UNIDIC_CWJ_FILEembed-model-unidic-cwjunidic-cwj
LINDERA_BUILD_DEPENDENCY_MODEL_UNIDIC_CSJ_FILEembed-model-unidic-csjunidic-csj
scripts/dependency/build_model.sh
export LINDERA_BUILD_DEPENDENCY_MODEL_IPADIC_FILE=$PWD/scripts/dependency/data/model/lindera-dependency-ipadic/dependency.model
cargo build --release -p lindera-cli --features embed-ipadic,embed-dependency-ipadic

  • A build from the repository needs it. The repository has no pin of a published model, and the model cannot be trained by the build script, so the build stops without the variable:

    Error: LinderaError { kind: Args, source: lindera-dependency-ipadic is embedded from a release of Lindera, and a build from the repository has none to take it from: build the model with scripts/dependency/build_model.sh of the Lindera repository, and set LINDERA_BUILD_DEPENDENCY_MODEL_IPADIC_FILE to the file }

  • A crate from crates.io pins the archive of its release, and embeds that without the variable. With the variable it embeds the file named, and downloads nothing.

  • The file is embedded as it is. What it holds is checked when the program asks for the model, not by the build.

  • Changing the variable, or the file it names, reruns the build script.

  • LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_PUBLISHED_BASE_URL names a mirror for the pinned archive too: it is on the page of the release, as the dictionaries are.

  • A documentation build (DOCS_RS) embeds an empty file, and reads neither.

See The model for IPADIC.

DOCS_RS

The DOCS_RS environment variable is automatically set by docs.rs when building documentation. When this variable is detected, Lindera creates dummy dictionary files instead of downloading actual dictionary data, allowing documentation to be built without network access or large file downloads.

Such a build ignores LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_CACHE_DIR: the dummy dictionaries are built in the build script's output directory, never in the cache, so a later build without DOCS_RS does not embed them.

This is primarily used internally by docs.rs and typically doesn't need to be set by users.

Runtime variables

LINDERA_CONFIG_FILE

The LINDERA_CONFIG_FILE environment variable names a YAML configuration file for the tokenizer, which TokenizerBuilder::new() reads. This allows you to configure tokenizer behavior without modifying Rust code.

export LINDERA_CONFIG_FILE=./resources/config/lindera.yml

LINDERA_CONFIG_PATH, the name of this variable up to v6, still works until v8.0.0, with a deprecation warning on standard error. When both are set, LINDERA_CONFIG_FILE is used.

See the Configuration section for details on the configuration format.

CLI variables

The lindera command reads these variables; see Commands of the Lindera CLI for the commands.

LINDERA_DICTIONARIES_DIR

The LINDERA_DICTIONARIES_DIR environment variable names the dictionaries directory: lindera download <name> installs the dictionary in <dictionaries directory>/<name>/, lindera list lists the dictionaries there, and the error for a dictionary name given to --dict or --system-dict names the path there. Without it, the directory is lindera/dictionaries in the OS's local data directory:

OSDefault location
Linux~/.local/share/lindera/dictionaries
macOS~/Library/Application Support/lindera/dictionaries
Windows%LOCALAPPDATA%\lindera\dictionaries

For example, with LINDERA_DICTIONARIES_DIR=/var/lindera/dict, lindera download ipadic installs to /var/lindera/dict/ipadic/. lindera list lists the dictionaries in the same directory.

LINDERA_DATA_DIR, the variable of the CLI before v7.0.0, keeps working until v8.0.0, with a warning on stderr: a value <dir> is read as LINDERA_DICTIONARIES_DIR=<dir>/dictionaries. For example, with LINDERA_DATA_DIR=/home/user/.local/share/lindera:

Warning: LINDERA_DATA_DIR is deprecated and will be removed in v8.0.0; set LINDERA_DICTIONARIES_DIR=/home/user/.local/share/lindera/dictionaries instead

When both are set, LINDERA_DICTIONARIES_DIR is used, and the warning says that LINDERA_DATA_DIR is ignored. Neither variable has to do with the build-time source cache variable LINDERA_BUILD_DICTIONARY_CACHE_DIR, or with LINDERA_DICTIONARIES_PATH, its former name, which v7.0.0 removed.

RUST_LOG

The RUST_LOG environment variable selects the messages that the CLI writes to standard error (see Warnings and log messages), in the syntax of env_logger:

  • Not set: warnings and errors.
  • RUST_LOG=error: errors only, which hides the warnings. RUST_LOG=off writes no log messages at all.
  • RUST_LOG=debug: also debugging messages, such as the files lindera build reads and writes.

The setting does not change standard output, and the error of a command that fails is written whatever the setting. The messages are colored when standard error is a terminal; RUST_LOG_STYLE=never turns the colors off.

Ruby gem build

LINDERA_FEATURES

The build of the Ruby gem, by gem install lindera or bundle exec rake compile, reads LINDERA_FEATURES, a comma-separated list of the Cargo features to enable. Without it, the gem builds with the default features (train) and no embedded dictionary.

LINDERA_FEATURES="embed-ipadic" gem install lindera

See Feature Flags of the Ruby binding for the features.

Quick Start

This example covers the basic usage of Lindera.

It will:

  • Create a segmenter in normal mode
  • Segment the input text
  • Output the tokens

This example uses the embed-ipadic feature, which downloads the IPADIC dictionary and embeds it into the binary automatically at build time — no manual dictionary download is required.

use std::borrow::Cow;

use lindera::dictionary::load_dictionary;
use lindera::mode::Mode;
use lindera::segmenter::Segmenter;
use lindera::LinderaResult;

fn main() -> LinderaResult<()> {
    let dictionary = load_dictionary("embedded://ipadic")?;
    let segmenter = Segmenter::new(Mode::Normal, dictionary, None);

    let text = "関西国際空港限定トートバッグ";
    let mut tokens = segmenter.segment(Cow::Borrowed(text))?;
    println!("text:\t{}", text);
    for token in tokens.iter_mut() {
        let details = token.details().join(",");
        println!("token:\t{}\t{}", token.surface.as_ref(), details);
    }

    Ok(())
}

The above example can be run as follows:

% cargo run --features embed-ipadic --example=segment

[!TIP] If you prefer not to embed the dictionary into the binary, download a pre-built IPADIC dictionary from GitHub Releases, extract it to a local directory (e.g., /path/to/ipadic), and call load_dictionary("/path/to/ipadic") instead — no embed-ipadic feature needed in that case. See Feature Flags for details.

You can see the result as follows:

text:   関西国際空港限定トートバッグ
token:  関西国際空港    名詞,固有名詞,組織,*,*,*,関西国際空港,カンサイコクサイクウコウ,カンサイコクサイクーコー
token:  限定    名詞,サ変接続,*,*,*,*,限定,ゲンテイ,ゲンテイ
token:  トートバッグ    名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,*,*,*

[!NOTE] Character filters, token filters, and the Tokenizer API are available as lindera::analysis (the analysis feature, enabled by default), so lindera = "7" already covers the whole analysis chain — no extra dependency is needed. With default-features = false you get the segmenter alone. See Lindera Analysis for details, and Migration v6 to v7 if you are upgrading from v6.

Examples

Lindera includes several example programs that demonstrate common use cases. The source code is available in the examples directory on GitHub (the tokenize* examples are in lindera-analysis/examples).

The tokenize* examples use the Tokenizer and filter APIs from lindera::analysis. They live in the lindera-analysis crate, hence -p lindera-analysis below.

All examples below are run with the embed-ipadic feature enabled, which downloads the IPADIC dictionary and embeds it into the binary automatically at build time — no manual dictionary download is required.

Available Examples

segment

Basic morphological segmentation with the Segmenter API — it needs only the segmenter, so it also works with default-features = false.

cargo run -p lindera --features=embed-ipadic --example=segment

tokenize

Basic tokenization using an external IPADIC dictionary. Segments input text and prints each token with its part-of-speech details.

cargo run -p lindera-analysis --features=embed-ipadic --example=tokenize

tokenize_with_user_dict

Tokenization with a user dictionary. Shows how to supplement the dictionary with custom entries for domain-specific terms.

cargo run -p lindera-analysis --features=embed-ipadic --example=tokenize_with_user_dict

tokenize_with_filters

Tokenization with character filters and token filters. Demonstrates the text processing pipeline, including Unicode normalization, part-of-speech filtering, and other transformations.

cargo run -p lindera-analysis --features=embed-ipadic --example=tokenize_with_filters

tokenize_with_config

Tokenization using a YAML configuration file. Shows how to configure the tokenizer declaratively instead of programmatically.

cargo run -p lindera-analysis --features=embed-ipadic --example=tokenize_with_config

Core Concepts

This section explains the fundamental concepts behind Lindera's morphological analysis system.

  • Morphological Analysis - How Lindera segments and analyzes text.
  • Dictionaries - Dictionary formats supported by Lindera.
  • Tokenization - Tokenization modes and N-Best analysis.
  • User Dictionary - Adding custom words with user dictionaries.
  • Filters - Pre-processing text and post-processing tokens with character and token filters.

Morphological Analysis

What is morphological analysis?

Morphological analysis is the process of breaking down text into its smallest meaningful units (morphemes) and identifying their grammatical properties. For languages like Japanese, Chinese, and Korean -- where words are not separated by spaces -- morphological analysis is an essential first step for natural language processing tasks such as search indexing, text classification, and machine translation.

How Lindera works

Lindera is a dictionary-based morphological analyzer. It uses a pre-compiled system dictionary containing known words along with their costs, and applies the Viterbi algorithm to find the optimal segmentation of input text.

The analysis process works as follows:

  1. Sentence splitting: Before building the lattice, Lindera splits the input text into sentences at delimiter characters (\n, \t, 。, 、) and processes one sentence at a time. If no delimiter appears within roughly 32 KiB of a sentence's start, Lindera forces a sentence boundary there anyway and logs a warning, to bound the lattice's memory and CPU cost. Up to the next \n or \t, each sentence continues from the words that end the previous one, so the result is, with few exceptions, the one a single lattice over that text gives (see Sentence Splitting). The forced cut can affect tokenization at the artificial cut point for pathological delimiter-free input, such as minified text or base64-encoded blobs.
  2. Lattice construction: Lindera scans each sentence and looks up all possible words in the dictionary at every position, building a directed acyclic graph (lattice) of candidate segmentations.
  3. Cost assignment: Each candidate word has an associated word cost (from the dictionary), and each pair of adjacent words has a connection cost (from the connection cost matrix).
  4. Optimal path search: The Viterbi algorithm finds the path through the lattice with the minimum total cost, producing the best segmentation.

Key terminology

TermDescription
Surface formThe actual text as it appears in the input (e.g., "食べ").
Part-of-speech (POS)The grammatical category of a word (e.g., noun, verb, particle). Lindera dictionaries provide hierarchical POS tags with up to four levels of subcategories.
ReadingThe pronunciation of a word, typically in Katakana for Japanese dictionaries.
Base formThe uninflected (dictionary) form of a word (e.g., "食べる" for the surface "食べ").
ConjugationInflection information for words that conjugate, consisting of a conjugation type and a conjugation form.

Cost-based segmentation

The Viterbi algorithm selects the segmentation path with the minimum total cost. The total cost of a path is the sum of:

  • Word costs: Each word in the dictionary has an associated cost. Lower cost means the word is more likely to appear. Common words tend to have lower costs, while rare words have higher costs.
  • Connection costs: The cost of connecting two adjacent words, determined by the right context ID of the left word and the left context ID of the right word.

The algorithm computes:

Total cost = sum of word costs + sum of connection costs

By minimizing this total cost, Lindera finds the most natural segmentation of the input text.

Connection cost matrix

The connection cost matrix stores the cost of transitioning from one word to another. It is a two-dimensional matrix indexed by:

  • The right context ID of the preceding word
  • The left context ID of the following word

These context IDs encode grammatical information about word boundaries. For example, the connection cost between a noun and a particle is typically low (natural sequence), while the connection cost between two verbs in base form might be high (unnatural sequence).

The connection cost matrix is compiled into binary format as part of the dictionary build process and is loaded at runtime for efficient lookup.

Dictionaries

Lindera supports various dictionaries for Japanese, Korean, and Chinese morphological analysis. Each dictionary is provided as a separate crate.

DictionaryLanguageCrateDescription
IPADICJapaneselindera-ipadicThe most common dictionary for Japanese
IPADIC NEologdJapaneselindera-ipadic-neologdIPADIC with neologisms (new words)
UniDicJapaneselindera-unidicUniform word unit definitions
UniDic CWJJapaneselindera-unidic-cwjUniDic ver.2025.12 from NINJAL, with accent and kana forms; 1.2 GB
UniDic CSJJapaneselindera-unidic-csjUniDic for spoken Japanese ver.2025.12 from NINJAL: UniDic CWJ's words with costs trained on conversation; 1.2 GB
SudachiDictJapaneselindera-sudachidictActively maintained vocabulary, updated several times a year upstream
ko-dicKoreanlindera-ko-dicKorean morphological analysis
CC-CEDICTChineselindera-cc-cedictChinese-English dictionary
JiebaChineselindera-jiebaJieba-based Chinese dictionary

Obtaining Dictionaries

Pre-built dictionaries are available for download from GitHub Releases. Download the dictionary archive for your target language and extract it to a local directory.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// Load an external dictionary from a local path
let dictionary = load_dictionary("/path/to/ipadic")?;
}

[!TIP] If you need a self-contained binary without external dictionary files, you can embed dictionaries using the embed-* feature flags and load them using the embedded:// scheme:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let dictionary = load_dictionary("embedded://ipadic")?;
}

See Feature Flags for details.

See each dictionary crate's documentation for format details, build instructions, and usage examples.

Tokenization

Lindera provides multiple tokenization modes and supports N-Best analysis for enumerating alternative segmentation candidates.

Tokenization modes

Normal mode

Normal mode performs standard tokenization based on dictionary entries. Compound words that exist as single entries in the dictionary are kept as-is.

Example -- tokenizing "関西国際空港限定トートバッグ" in Normal mode:

関西国際空港 | 限定 | トートバッグ

The compound noun "関西国際空港" (Kansai International Airport) is preserved as a single token because it exists as one entry in the dictionary.

Decompose mode

Decompose mode further breaks down compound nouns into their constituent parts, even when the compound exists as a dictionary entry.

Example -- tokenizing "関西国際空港限定トートバッグ" in Decompose mode:

関西 | 国際 | 空港 | 限定 | トートバッグ

The compound "関西国際空港" is decomposed into "関西", "国際", and "空港".

Selecting a mode

In Rust, specify the mode when creating a Segmenter:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use lindera::mode::Mode;
use lindera::segmenter::Segmenter;
use lindera::dictionary::load_dictionary;

let dictionary = load_dictionary("embedded://ipadic")?;

// Normal mode
let segmenter = Segmenter::new(Mode::Normal, dictionary, None);

// Decompose mode
let segmenter = Segmenter::new(Mode::Decompose(Default::default()), dictionary, None);
}

With the CLI, use the --mode flag:

echo "関西国際空港限定トートバッグ" | lindera tokenize --dict embedded://ipadic --mode normal
echo "関西国際空港限定トートバッグ" | lindera tokenize --dict embedded://ipadic --mode decompose

[!NOTE] The embedded:// scheme requires lindera-cli to be built with the corresponding embed-* feature (e.g. cargo install lindera-cli --features=embed-ipadic). A default build of lindera-cli does not enable any embed-* feature, and passing --dict embedded://ipadic without it fails with Invalid dictionary scheme: embedded.

N-Best tokenization

N-Best tokenization enumerates the top N tokenization candidates ordered by total path cost (lower cost = better segmentation). This is useful when the best result is ambiguous, or when you want to explore alternative interpretations of the input text.

Algorithm

N-Best tokenization is based on the Forward-DP Backward-A* algorithm, which is compatible with MeCab's N-Best implementation. The forward pass computes optimal costs using dynamic programming, and the backward pass uses A* search to enumerate paths in order of increasing total cost.

As in 1-best tokenization, the input is first split into sentences, and the sentences up to each \n or \t form a segment (see Sentence Splitting). Each segment is searched on its own: within it, the context is carried across 、 and 。, so its paths are the N best paths of one lattice over the segment. Every candidate segments the whole input: it takes one path in each segment, and its cost is the sum of those paths' costs. The candidates are the N cheapest of these combinations.

With unique, the backward search runs over word boundaries instead of paths: a segmentation has one path per choice of dictionary entry for each of its words, which can be millions for a short line, and the search takes each segmentation once, with its cheapest path, without going through the others.

Parameters

The tokenize_nbest method accepts the following parameters:

ParameterTypeDescription
text&strThe text to tokenize.
nusizeNumber of N-best results to return.
uniqueboolWhen true, deduplicates results that produce the same word boundary positions: each result is the cheapest path of its word boundaries.
cost_thresholdOption<i64>When Some(threshold), only returns candidates with cost within best_cost + threshold, where best_cost is the cost of the first candidate (both are totals over the whole input).

Rust API example

use lindera::dictionary::load_dictionary;
use lindera::mode::Mode;
use lindera::segmenter::Segmenter;
use lindera::analysis::tokenizer::Tokenizer;
use lindera::LinderaResult;

fn main() -> LinderaResult<()> {
    let dictionary = load_dictionary("embedded://ipadic")?;
    let segmenter = Segmenter::new(Mode::Normal, dictionary, None);
    let tokenizer = Tokenizer::new(segmenter);

    let text = "すもももももももものうち";

    // Get top 3 tokenization results
    let results = tokenizer.tokenize_nbest(text, 3, false, None)?;

    for (rank, (tokens, cost)) in results.iter().enumerate() {
        println!("--- NBEST {} (cost={}) ---", rank + 1, cost);
        for token in tokens {
            let details = token.details().join(",");
            println!("{}\t{}", token.surface.as_ref(), details);
        }
    }

    Ok(())
}

Output:

--- NBEST 1 (cost=21245) ---
すもも  名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,すもも,スモモ,スモモ
も      助詞,係助詞,*,*,*,*,も,モ,モ
もも    名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,もも,モモ,モモ
も      助詞,係助詞,*,*,*,*,も,モ,モ
もも    名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,もも,モモ,モモ
の      助詞,連体化,*,*,*,*,の,ノ,ノ
うち    名詞,非自立,副詞可能,*,*,*,うち,ウチ,ウチ
--- NBEST 2 (cost=24541) ---
...

CLI example

echo "すもももももももものうち" | lindera tokenize --dict embedded://ipadic -N 3

Lattice reuse

For repeated tokenization, you can reuse a Lattice to reduce memory allocations:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use lindera::dictionary::Lattice;

let mut lattice = Lattice::default();
let results = tokenizer.tokenize_nbest_with_lattice(text, &mut lattice, 3, false, None)?;
}

At the segmenter level, SegmentWorker (created via Segmenter::new_worker) packages this pattern into a session object that owns the lattice and scratch buffers, and additionally bounds retained memory with an automatic shrink policy. See the Segmenter page for details.

User Dictionary

A user dictionary is a supplementary dictionary that allows you to register custom words alongside the system dictionary. This is useful for domain-specific terms, brand names, proper nouns, or any words that are not in the default system dictionary.

CSV format

The simplest user dictionary format is a CSV file with three columns:

<surface>,<part_of_speech>,<reading>

Example CSV content

東京スカイツリー,カスタム名詞,トウキョウスカイツリー
東武スカイツリーライン,カスタム名詞,トウブスカイツリーライン
とうきょうスカイツリー駅,カスタム名詞,トウキョウスカイツリーエキ

The surface (the first column) is used exactly as written: whitespace at its start or end is part of the word, and a surface may consist of whitespace only (IPADIC registers U+3000 this way). Only an empty surface is skipped. The same applies to the lexicon CSV files of a system dictionary built with lindera build.

An entry that ends with whitespace keeps it in its token, as in MeCab, even when whitespace is skipped in the lattice (the default for every bundled dictionary except SudachiDict, see Whitespace Handling). With whitespace skipped, however, an entry that starts with whitespace of the dictionary's SPACE category, or consists of such whitespace only, never matches, because no word starts on skipped whitespace. U+3000 is not in the SPACE category, so IPADIC's U+3000 entry still matches.

Each dictionary type (IPADIC, UniDic, ko-dic, etc.) also supports a detailed CSV format with full control over context IDs, costs, and all feature fields. See the Dictionaries section for the detailed format of each dictionary type.

Tied entries

Two entries tie when they have the same surface, the same left and right context IDs and the same cost: every path costs the same with either of them. A user entry that ties with a system entry is chosen over it, so a detailed entry that copies the surface, the context IDs and the cost of a system entry, for example to give the word another reading, takes its place in the output. MeCab chooses the system entry instead. Among tied user entries, the first row is chosen, as in MeCab (before v7, the last row was; see Migrating from v6 to v7). Simple entries get the cost and the context IDs from the dictionary's metadata.json (default_word_cost, default_left_context_id and default_right_context_id: -10000, 0 and 0 for IPADIC), so they practically never tie with a system entry.

Context IDs

The left and right context IDs of a detailed entry must address a cell of the connection matrix of the system dictionary it is used with: the left context ID must be below the second value of that dictionary's matrix.def header, and the right context ID below the first, the bounds lindera build applies to the system dictionary itself. IPADIC's matrix is 1316 x 1316, for example.

A user dictionary built from CSV together with its system dictionary is checked row by row as it is built, and the first row outside the matrix fails with an error that names its CSV line and surface:

  • lindera build --user when --system-dict names the system dictionary (DictionaryBuilder::with_system_matrix in the Rust API; see Context ID check)
  • a .csv user dictionary that the configuration names (Segmenter::from_config, TokenizerBuilder), that lindera tokenize --user-dict names, or that the TokenizerBuilder of the Python, Node.js, Ruby and PHP bindings is given by path
  • the loaders that load a user dictionary for a loaded system dictionary: load_user_dictionary_for in the Rust API, Python and Ruby, loadUserDictionaryFor in Node.js, Lindera\Dictionary::loadUserFor in PHP, and loadUserDictionaryFromBytesFor in WebAssembly
  • the builders that build a user dictionary for a loaded system dictionary: build_user_dictionary_for in Python and Ruby, buildUserDictionaryFor in Node.js, and Lindera\Dictionary::buildUserFor in PHP

For example, with a userdic.csv whose first row lies inside IPADIC's matrix and whose second row has the left context ID 60000:

$ echo 東京スカイツリーへ行く | lindera tokenize -d embedded://ipadic -u userdic.csv
Error: LinderaError { kind: Args, source: LinderaError(kind=Parse, source=failed to build tokenizer: LinderaError(kind=Content, source=user dictionary line 2 (surface: '東京スカイツリー'): left context id 60000 is out of range for the connection matrix (matrix.def size 1316 1316; left context ids must be below 1316)))

Otherwise the user dictionary is built without the system dictionary: a .bin that lindera build --user wrote without --system-dict or that a builder of the bindings wrote with metadata only (build_user_dictionary in Python and Ruby, buildUserDictionary in Node.js, Lindera\Dictionary::buildUser in PHP), or a user dictionary loaded with metadata only (load_user_dictionary in the Rust API, Python and Ruby, loadUserDictionary in Node.js, Lindera\Dictionary::loadUser in PHP, loadUserDictionaryFromBytes in WebAssembly). Its IDs are checked when the two dictionaries are combined: Segmenter::try_new, the configuration path, lindera tokenize --user-dict, and the Tokenizer constructors and builders of the language bindings return an error for the first entry outside the matrix. The error names the entry by its word id, which counts the rows from 0 in the order of their surfaces, and by its detail fields. The .bin built from the userdic.csv above gives:

$ echo 東京スカイツリーへ行く | lindera tokenize -d embedded://ipadic -u user_dict/userdic.bin
Error: LinderaError { kind: Args, source: LinderaError(kind=Parse, source=failed to build tokenizer: LinderaError(kind=Content, source=user dictionary entry 1 (名詞,固有名詞,一般,*,*,*,東京スカイツリー,トウキョウスカイツリー,トウキョウスカイツリー): left context id 60000 is out of range for the connection matrix (matrix.def size 1316 1316; left context ids must be below 1316)))

Segmenter::new does not check the IDs: an entry outside the matrix then makes segmentation panic when the entry matches the input. Before v7.0.0, every path behaved this way. Simple entries are checked too; they get the context IDs that the metadata.json they are built with sets (default_left_context_id and default_right_context_id, 0 in every bundled dictionary).

Rust API example

use std::fs::File;
use std::path::PathBuf;

use lindera::dictionary::{Metadata, load_dictionary, load_user_dictionary};
use lindera::error::LinderaErrorKind;
use lindera::mode::Mode;
use lindera::segmenter::Segmenter;
use lindera::analysis::tokenizer::Tokenizer;
use lindera::LinderaResult;

fn main() -> LinderaResult<()> {
    let user_dict_path = PathBuf::from(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR"))
        .join("../resources")
        .join("user_dict")
        .join("ipadic_simple_userdic.csv");

    let metadata_file = PathBuf::from(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR"))
        .join("../lindera-ipadic")
        .join("metadata.json");
    let metadata: Metadata = serde_json::from_reader(
        File::open(metadata_file)
            .map_err(|err| LinderaErrorKind::Io.with_error(anyhow::anyhow!(err)))
            .unwrap(),
    )
    .map_err(|err| LinderaErrorKind::Io.with_error(anyhow::anyhow!(err)))
    .unwrap();

    let dictionary = load_dictionary("embedded://ipadic")?;
    let user_dictionary = load_user_dictionary(user_dict_path.to_str().unwrap(), &metadata)?;
    // `try_new` checks the user dictionary's context IDs against the
    // dictionary's connection matrix (see "Context IDs" above).
    let segmenter = Segmenter::try_new(
        Mode::Normal,
        dictionary,
        Some(user_dictionary), // Using the loaded user dictionary
    )?;

    // Create a tokenizer.
    let tokenizer = Tokenizer::new(segmenter);

    // Tokenize a text.
    let text = "東京スカイツリーの最寄り駅はとうきょうスカイツリー駅です";
    let mut tokens = tokenizer.tokenize(text)?;

    // Print the text and tokens.
    println!("text:\t{}", text);
    for token in tokens.iter_mut() {
        let details = token.details().join(",");
        println!("token:\t{}\t{}", token.surface.as_ref(), details);
    }

    Ok(())
}

Output:

text:   東京スカイツリーの最寄り駅はとうきょうスカイツリー駅です
token:  東京スカイツリー        カスタム名詞,*,*,*,*,*,*,トウキョウスカイツリー,*
token:  の      助詞,連体化,*,*,*,*,の,ノ,ノ
token:  最寄り駅        名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,最寄り駅,モヨリエキ,モヨリエキ
token:  は      助詞,係助詞,*,*,*,*,は,ハ,ワ
token:  とうきょうスカイツリー駅        カスタム名詞,*,*,*,*,*,*,トウキョウスカイツリーエキ,*
token:  です    助動詞,*,*,*,特殊・デス,基本形,です,デス,デス

Note that the base_form field (the 7th CSV/detail field) is * rather than the surface form. The simple three-column user-dictionary schema only supplies surface, part_of_speech, and reading — every other field, including base_form, is filled with the dictionary's metadata.default_field_value (* for IPADIC).

Building a user dictionary with CLI

You can build a user dictionary from CSV to binary format using the CLI:

lindera build --src <user_dictionary.csv> --dest <dest_dir> --metadata <metadata.json> --user [--system-dict <system_dictionary>]

With --system-dict, the build checks the context IDs against the system dictionary the user dictionary is for (see Context IDs).

Binary vs CSV user dictionary

  • CSV format: Loaded and parsed at runtime. Convenient for development and small dictionaries.
  • Binary format: Pre-compiled for faster loading. Recommended for production use with large user dictionaries.

Both formats can be specified when creating a Segmenter. The binary format skips the CSV parsing step, resulting in faster startup times.

Filters

Lindera's analysis pipeline (the Tokenizer in lindera::analysis, provided by the lindera-analysis crate) has two extension points around the segmenter: character filters, which transform the raw input text before tokenization, and token filters, which transform the list of tokens after tokenization.

Input Text
  --> Character Filters (preprocessing)
  --> Tokenization
  --> Token Filters (postprocessing)
  --> Output Tokens

Character filters

Character filters preprocess the input text before it reaches the segmenter. They're typically used to normalize text so that tokenization is more consistent -- for example, converting full-width characters to half-width, canonicalizing Unicode representations, or expanding Japanese iteration marks into their repeated form. Because a character filter can change the length of the text, Lindera tracks every transformation it makes and corrects each token's byte offsets back to positions in the original, unfiltered text.

Token filters

Token filters postprocess the list of tokens produced by the segmenter. They're typically used to normalize or reduce the token list for search and analysis -- for example, replacing a token with its base (dictionary) form, converting a token's surface text between hiragana and katakana, removing tokens by part-of-speech tag, or removing stop words.

Configuring filters

Every filter -- character or token -- is identified by a kind string and configured with a JSON args object of filter-specific parameters. Filters run in the order they're added, and there are two ways to add them:

  • YAML configuration file: list filters under the character_filters and token_filters keys.

    character_filters:
  - kind: unicode_normalize
    args:
      kind: nfkc

token_filters:
  - kind: japanese_base_form

  • Rust API: append filters to a Tokenizer, in order, with append_character_filter and append_token_filter.

    #![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// Character filters run first, transforming the raw input text;
// token filters run last, transforming the resulting token list.
tokenizer
    .append_character_filter(BoxCharacterFilter::from(unicode_normalize_char_filter))
    .append_token_filter(BoxTokenFilter::from(japanese_base_form_filter));
}

Available filters

Lindera ships 4 character filters and 21 token filters, covering Japanese, Korean, and general-purpose text normalization:

CategoryFilters
Character filtersunicode_normalize, japanese_iteration_mark, mapping, regex
Token filters -- normalizationjapanese_base_form, japanese_reading_form, korean_reading_form, japanese_kana, japanese_katakana_stem, japanese_number, korean_number, mapping, remove_diacritical_mark, lowercase, uppercase
Token filters -- tag-based filteringjapanese_keep_tags, japanese_stop_tags, korean_keep_tags, korean_stop_tags
Token filters -- word-based filteringkeep_words, stop_words
Token filters -- structural transformationjapanese_compound_word, korean_compound_word, korean_decompound, length

See the Filters reference for what each filter does, its parameters, and runnable YAML and Rust API examples.

Lindera CRF

Lindera CRF is a pure Rust implementation of Conditional Random Fields (CRFs), forked from rucrf. It provides a trainer and an estimator for CRFs with support for lattice structures.

Key Features

  • Lattices with variable length edges
  • L1, L2, and Elastic Net regularization
  • Multi-threaded training
  • Zero-copy deserialization with rkyv
  • no_std support via --no-default-features --features alloc

Contents

  • Architecture -- Internal structure and key components
  • API Reference -- API documentation

Changes from rucrf

  • Serialization backend: Switched from bincode to rkyv for zero-copy deserialization
  • Elastic Net regularization: Added Regularization::ElasticNet combining L1 and L2 penalties
  • Default regularization: Trainer::new regularizes with L2 and DEFAULT_LAMBDA (1.0), the objective of MeCab's learner with its default -c 1.0; rucrf's default is L1 with 0.1
  • Rust 2024 edition: Updated to Rust 2024 edition
  • Dependency updates: Updated argmin, argmin-math, hashbrown, etc.

Architecture

Module Structure

lindera-crf/src/
├── lib.rs                # Public API re-exports
├── bigram_table.rs       # Bigram weight indices of the training lattices
├── console.rs            # Side output written without panicking (write, write_line)
├── feature.rs            # FeatureSet, FeatureProvider
├── lattice.rs            # Edge, Node, Lattice
├── model.rs              # RawModel, MergedModel, Model trait
├── trainer.rs            # Trainer, Regularization, StopReason, TrainingStats
├── errors.rs             # Error types
├── forward_backward.rs   # Forward-backward algorithm
├── math.rs               # Mathematical utilities (logsumexp)
├── optimizers.rs         # Declares the optimizers module
├── optimizers/
│   └── lbfgs.rs          # L-BFGS optimization
└── utils.rs              # Utility traits

Key Components

FeatureProvider / FeatureSet

Manage per-label feature sets. Each FeatureSet holds unigram features and left/right bigram features for a given label (feature IDs only, no weights). FeatureProvider maps label IDs to FeatureSet instances. Weights are held separately, on RawModel (weights, unigram_weight_indices, bigram_weight_indices).

The bigram feature IDs are held in Arc<[Option<NonZeroU32>]>, so labels with the same bigram features can share one list: FeatureSet::with_shared_bigrams takes the lists as Arcs, while FeatureSet::new copies the slices it is given. When training drops the unused features, it filters each shared list once, and the labels that shared the list share the filtered one. lindera-trainer shares the lists among the labels whose rewritten left and right features are the same (#1263).

Lattice / Edge / Node

Lattice structure with variable-length edges for sequence labeling. Edge represents a candidate span with a label, while Node aggregates edges at a given position. The Lattice is constructed from input data and used by the model to find the best path.

Trainer

Trains a CRF model using L-BFGS optimization (OWL-QN when the regularization has an L1 part) with configurable regularization. As in MeCab's learner and libLBFGS, the first line search starts at a step of 1 / |d|, d being the first search direction, and every later one at a step of 1. The trainer accepts labeled lattice examples, computes the loss and its gradient via the forward-backward algorithm, and iteratively updates model weights. Trainer::train returns the trained RawModel; Trainer::train_with_stats also returns a TrainingStats with:

  • iterations: the number of iterations that ran, which is the maximum set with Trainer::max_iter when that stopped training, and fewer when the optimizer stopped earlier.
  • evaluations: the number of evaluations of the loss and its gradient, each one forward-backward pass over every lattice, line-search trials included.
  • stop_reason: why the optimizer stopped, a StopReason.

The optimizer stops at the first of these:

  • StopReason::Converged: the relative change of the objective, |previous - current| / |previous|, stayed below the tolerance set with Trainer::eta for 3 iterations in a row, or the optimizer stopped near the optimum, where the norm of the gradient (the pseudo-gradient for OWL-QN) is under 1e-5 times its norm at the initial weights, or vanishes. The default tolerance, DEFAULT_ETA (5e-5), is the default eta of MeCab's learner, which applies the same test to every evaluation, line-search trials included, where Lindera counts iterations. Trainer::eta(0.0) turns the test off. Near the optimum the objective changes by less than its rounding, and whether an iteration then leaves it unchanged or a line search fails depends on the platform; either is Converged there.
  • StopReason::NoProgress: an iteration left the objective unchanged far from the optimum, where the norm of the gradient was still at least 1e-5 times its norm at the initial weights. When this happens after a few iterations, the model is barely trained.
  • StopReason::MaxIterations: the cap set with Trainer::max_iter.
  • StopReason::LineSearchFailed: the line search of an iteration failed far from the optimum, where the norm of the gradient at the best weights of the run was still at least 1e-5 times its norm at the initial weights. The weights are the best ones of the run. A search direction with a component that is not finite, which the optimizer builds from a step that left the gradient unchanged, fails the line search too.

While it trains, the optimizer writes the solver's name, L-BFGS, and then a line per iteration to standard error, such as iter: 1, cost: 0.5948643217470097, best_cost: 0.5948643217470097, gamma: 0.47689090558496994: the number of the iteration, its cost, the best cost so far, and the solver's key-value pairs, sorted by key. It writes them on the training thread through console::write_line, as a write to a blocking stream would: while the stream is full and non-blocking, as Node.js makes the standard streams of a node --test child, it waits until the stream takes the line, trying again after 1 ms, doubling up to 50 ms, and a line that the stream can no longer take, such as a pipe whose reader has exited, is dropped. It never panics, so the training gives the same result whatever happens to its output (#1312). lindera_trainer writes its progress and warnings with the same function. So do lindera-analysis, for its warning about the configuration variables (#1315), and lindera-cli, for its own messages on standard error (#1329), which use lindera-crf with only its console feature. console::write writes in the same way without a newline, for the progress line that lindera download rewrites on a terminal.

Regularization

Configurable regularization strategies:

  • L1: Sparse models via L1 penalty
  • L2: Smooth models via L2 penalty
  • ElasticNet: Combines L1 and L2 with a configurable l1_ratio

Trainer::new uses L2 with DEFAULT_LAMBDA (1.0): the objective of MeCab's learner with its default -c 1.0. MeCab adds ‖w‖² / (2C), so the coefficient is 1 / C in general.

Model (trait)

Interface for searching the best path through a lattice. Two implementations are provided:

  • RawModel: Stores weights in a flat vector indexed by feature ID
  • MergedModel: Optimized for inference; merges feature weights into a compact representation serializable with rkyv, using MergedFeatureSet as its per-label element type

MergedFeatureSet holds the pre-summed unigram weight for a label, along with its left_id/right_id bigram connection IDs into MergedModel's bigram weight matrix.

RawModel::unigram_weight computes that sum for a list of unigram feature IDs, and merge calls it for every label. A feature without a weight adds nothing, so it also weighs the features of an entry that was not a label in training: lindera-trainer uses it for the cost of a user lexicon entry.

Forward-backward Algorithm

Computes alpha (forward) and beta (backward) values over the lattice. Used during training to calculate the loss and the expected feature counts. One pass over a lattice yields both its loss and its share of the gradient. The optimizer keeps the result for the last parameter vector, because argmin's L-BFGS asks for the cost and the gradient of the same point in two calls.

Before the optimizer starts, a bigram table records, for every pair of edges that meet in the lattices, the weight indices of their bigram features, in the order the evaluation adds them; labels with the same bigram feature IDs share the entries. The evaluations read the indices from the table instead of looking each bigram feature up in a map, and add the same weights in the same order, so the trained weights do not change.

Feature Flags

FeatureDescriptionDefault
allocAlloc support for no_stdNo*
stdStandard library support (implies alloc)No*
consoleWriting to the standard streams without panicking (console::write, console::write_line), without the training (implies std)No*
trainTraining functionality (L-BFGS, multi-threading, progress lines; implies console)Yes

* Not listed directly in default, but transitively enabled by train (which is on by default and enables console, which enables std, which in turn enables alloc) -- so alloc/std/console are active in a default build.

API Reference

The API reference is available. Please see following URL:

  • lindera-crf

Lindera Dictionary

Lindera Dictionary is the base library for morphological analysis dictionaries. It provides dictionary loading, building, and Viterbi-based segmentation. CRF-based dictionary training lives in the separate lindera-trainer crate. Through the lindera facade its modules are available under lindera::dictionary — lindera::dictionary::core (the dictionary data structures), lindera::dictionary::builder, lindera::dictionary::viterbi, and so on — so a direct lindera-dictionary dependency is rarely needed.

Key Features

  • Dictionary loading from filesystem or embedded data
  • Dictionary building from MeCab-format CSV source files
  • Viterbi algorithm for optimal segmentation
  • N-best path generation (Forward-DP Backward-A*)
  • Memory-mapped file support

Contents

  • Architecture -- Internal structure and key components
  • API Reference -- API documentation

Architecture

Module Structure

lindera-dictionary/src/
├── lib.rs               # Public API
├── dictionary.rs        # Dictionary, UserDictionary
├── builder.rs           # DictionaryBuilder
├── loader.rs            # DictionaryLoader trait, FSDictionaryLoader
├── viterbi.rs           # Lattice, Edge, Viterbi segmentation
├── nbest.rs             # NBestGenerator, UniqueNBestGenerator (Forward-DP Backward-A*)
├── mode.rs              # Mode (Normal/Decompose), Penalty
├── error.rs             # LinderaError, LinderaErrorKind
├── assets.rs            # Download and file management
├── macros.rs            # embedded_dictionary! macro shared by dictionary crates
├── dictionary/
│   ├── character_definition.rs    # Character type definitions
│   ├── connection_cost_matrix.rs  # Connection cost matrix
│   ├── context_id_map.rs          # ContextIdMap: connection-cost context-ID remap
│   ├── prefix_dictionary.rs       # Prefix dictionary (char-wise double-array trie)
│   ├── unknown_dictionary.rs      # Unknown word handling
│   ├── metadata.rs                # Dictionary metadata
│   └── schema.rs                  # Schema definitions

Key Components

Dictionary / UserDictionary

Main data structures holding the compiled dictionary data. A Dictionary contains the character definitions, connection cost matrix, prefix dictionary, and unknown word dictionary. The prefix dictionary is a char-wise double-array trie, built with crawdad at build time and walked in place over its serialized bytes at runtime — loading it is an O(1) header check, not a deserialization pass. UserDictionary allows users to add custom vocabulary on top of the system dictionary; unlike the system dictionary, it still uses a daachorse automaton inside its rkyv-archived .bin files.

DictionaryBuilder

Fluent API for building dictionaries from source CSV files. It compiles MeCab-format dictionary sources into the binary format used at runtime. Its four build stages (metadata, unknown dictionary, prefix dictionary, connection cost matrix) run concurrently on scoped threads on non-wasm targets, falling back to a sequential build on wasm (which has no OS threads); the concurrent path has higher peak memory, since all four stages' working sets are held at once.

DictionaryLoader / FSDictionaryLoader

DictionaryLoader is a trait for loading compiled dictionaries. FSDictionaryLoader is the filesystem-based implementation that reads dictionary files from a directory, with optional memory-mapped file support.

Embedded Dictionary Macro

The embedded_dictionary! macro (lindera-dictionary/src/macros.rs, #[macro_export]) generates the boilerplate each dictionary crate needs to bake its compiled dictionary into the binary: a load() function that reads the dictionary components via include_bytes! and a loader struct implementing DictionaryLoader. Every dictionary crate's embedded.rs (lindera-ipadic, lindera-ipadic-neologd, lindera-unidic, lindera-ko-dic, lindera-cc-cedict, lindera-jieba) invokes this macro instead of duplicating the loading logic.

Viterbi (Lattice, Edge)

Builds a lattice of candidate tokens from the input text and finds the optimal segmentation path using the Viterbi algorithm. Each Edge in the lattice represents a candidate token with associated costs (word cost + connection cost).

NBestGenerator

Generates N-best segmentation paths using the Forward-DP Backward-A* algorithm. This enables applications to consider alternative segmentations beyond the single best path.

UniqueNBestGenerator

Generates the N-best distinct segmentations: for each sequence of word boundaries, its cheapest path, in ascending order of cost. Unique N-best (unique, --nbest-unique) uses it. A segmentation has one path per choice of dictionary entry for each of its words, which can be millions of paths for a short line, so the search runs backward over suffixes of word boundaries instead of paths: one search node holds every candidate of a span, and its cost is exact, so each segmentation comes out once and the work grows with the number of results and the length of the line, not with the number of paths. The first result is the 1-best path, and of identical entries (same surface, context ids and cost) every result holds the first CSV row, as the 1-best path does.

Mode

Controls tokenization behavior:

  • Normal: Standard tokenization using the optimal Viterbi path
  • Decompose: Further splits compound nouns based on configurable Penalty thresholds

Dictionary Format Version

A built dictionary directory records the on-disk layout it was written in, as format_version in metadata.json. DictionaryBuilder::build_metadata stamps the value from DICTIONARY_FORMAT_VERSION (lindera-dictionary/src/dictionary/metadata.rs) — the builder is the only thing that can state truthfully what it just wrote, so a value in the source metadata.json is ignored. Loading a dictionary directory checks the recorded version and fails with an actionable message if it does not match.

The check matters because most artifacts have no header of their own: matrix.mtx, dict.vals and dict.words are raw arrays, so a dictionary from an older layout that happens to be a plausible length decodes into garbage rather than failing. A source metadata.json — the hand-written kind checked into each dictionary crate — describes build inputs, carries no format_version, and is never format-checked.

build_metadata stamps lindera_version, the version of Lindera that built the dictionary, in the same way. Loading does not check it: lindera list shows it, and lindera download downloads a dictionary again when it differs from the CLI's version. Dictionaries built before v7.0.0 do not have it.

Bump DICTIONARY_FORMAT_VERSION on any change to the bytes of a built artifact. That includes upgrading a dependency whose serialized form is written verbatim (crawdad for dict.trie, rkyv for char_def.bin and unk.bin, daachorse inside user dictionary .bin files), which is easy to overlook because no line of this crate changes. The build cache is keyed on the format version for exactly that reason.

The current format version is 3. Version 2 (v6.0.0) replaced the system prefix dictionary's byte-wise daachorse Aho-Corasick automaton (dict.da) with a char-wise double-array trie (dict.trie) plus a u32 prefix-sum index (dict.valsidx). Version 3 (v7.0.0) lists each code point's default category first in its char_def.bin row, followed by its other categories in category id order, because unknown words come from the default category only, as in MeCab; a version 2 row would silently give the wrong default category. Version 3 also covers the earlier 7.0.0 changes to what the builder writes (see Migrating from v6 to v7), and a later one, made before any release read version 3: char_def.bin records the format of char.def and, in Sudachi's format, the flags of each row (#1388). Dictionaries at version 2 or earlier are rejected at load time with an actionable error. User dictionary .bin files were not affected by that change — but they are written by daachorse, so a daachorse upgrade does invalidate them, which is exactly why it belongs in the list above.

Context ID Remapping

Dictionary metadata (lindera-dictionary/src/dictionary/metadata.rs) carries a connection_id_mapping: bool flag and an optional context_id_map: Option<ContextIdMap>. When a dictionary crate (e.g. lindera-unidic) enables connection_id_mapping, DictionaryBuilder relabels the connection matrix's left/right context IDs by access frequency at build time, so that frequently-used connection-cost cells cluster together for better cache locality; DictionaryBuilder::with_context_id_freq attaches an optional bundled frequency histogram used to rank the IDs, and the remap itself is computed in lindera-dictionary/src/builder/context_id_remap.rs. ContextIdMap (lindera-dictionary/src/dictionary/context_id_map.rs) holds the resulting left/right permutation and is persisted into the built metadata.json so the same mapping can be reapplied later. Because user dictionaries are always compiled in the original, un-remapped ID space, UserDictionary::remap_context_ids (lindera-dictionary/src/dictionary.rs) uses the persisted ContextIdMap to relabel a user dictionary's context IDs into the same space as the system dictionary it is attached to. The remap is a bijective relabeling, so it does not change tokenization output, only lookup locality.

Training

The CRF-based dictionary training pipeline lives in the separate lindera-trainer crate, which builds on this crate's runtime types. See the training pipeline documentation for details.

Feature Flags

FeatureDescriptionDefault
mmapMemory-mapped file support for filesystem-based dictionary loading (the word-list files, the connection-cost matrix, and the trie all stay lazily paged; nothing is fully materialized at load)Yes
build_rsHTTP download for dictionary sourcesNo
ctxfreqExperimental: instruments connection-matrix access-frequency profiling, used to build the context-ID frequency remapNo

API Reference

The API reference is available. Please see following URL:
