Configuration

Lindera is able to read YAML format configuration files. Specify the path to the following file in the environment variable LINDERA_CONFIG_FILE. You can use it easily without having to code the behavior of the tokenizer in Rust code.

segmenter:
  mode: "normal"
  dictionary: "embedded://ipadic"
  # user_dictionary: "./resources/user_dict/ipadic_simple_userdic.csv"
  # keep_whitespace: false
  # skip_whitespace: false # skip whitespace in the lattice, as MeCab does; on by default except for SudachiDict. false keeps whitespace nodes (pre-v7)
  # use_mmap: false # only meaningful for filesystem (non-embedded://) dictionaries
  # max_grouping_len: 24 # cap on unknown-word grouping; omit or 0 for unbounded
  # unknown_word_ladder: true # emit shorter unknown-word candidates (default: true)
  # break_characters: "・" # no unknown word, nor in decompose mode any system-dictionary word, crosses a boundary of these characters (default: "・"); "" splits as MeCab does
  # space_penalty: false # left-space penalty (Korean); on by default for dictionaries that ship rules (ko-dic). false turns it off, an object gives explicit rules

character_filters:
  - kind: "unicode_normalize"
    args:
      kind: "nfkc"
  - kind: "japanese_iteration_mark"
    args:
      normalize_kanji: true
      normalize_kana: true
  - kind: mapping
    args:
       mapping:
         リンデラ: Lindera

token_filters:
  - kind: "japanese_compound_word"
    args:
      # Merge the numeral tokens only. A counter merged into the number token keeps japanese_number from converting it.
      tags:
        - "名詞,数"
      new_tag: "名詞,数"
  - kind: "japanese_number"
    args:
      tags:
        - "名詞,数"
  - kind: "japanese_stop_tags"
    args:
      tags:
        - "接続詞"
        - "助詞"
        - "助詞,格助詞"
        - "助詞,格助詞,一般"
        - "助詞,格助詞,引用"
        - "助詞,格助詞,連語"
        - "助詞,係助詞"
        - "助詞,副助詞"
        - "助詞,間投助詞"
        - "助詞,並立助詞"
        - "助詞,終助詞"
        - "助詞,副助詞／並立助詞／終助詞"
        - "助詞,連体化"
        - "助詞,副詞化"
        - "助詞,特殊"
        - "助動詞"
        - "記号"
        - "記号,一般"
        - "記号,読点"
        - "記号,句点"
        - "記号,空白"
        - "記号,括弧閉"
        - "その他,間投"
        - "フィラー"
        - "非言語音"
  - kind: "japanese_katakana_stem"
    args:
      min: 3
  - kind: "remove_diacritical_mark"
    args:
      japanese: false

Segmenter Options

KeyTypeDefaultDescription
modestring"normal"Segmentation mode: "normal" or "decompose"
dictionarystring(required)Dictionary URI, e.g. "embedded://ipadic"
user_dictionarystring(none)Path to a user dictionary
keep_whitespaceboolfalseEmit whitespace tokens. Whitespace then also stays in the lattice, so the other tokens can differ from those of the default output, which skips whitespace as MeCab does
skip_whitespacebool(the dictionary's: true, false for SudachiDict)With keep_whitespace false, skip whitespace in the lattice so the words on either side connect directly, as in MeCab. false keeps whitespace in the lattice as a node of its own (a whitespace dictionary entry or the SPACE unknown word), as before v7; with ko-dic, whose connection costs for that node are all zero, every space then resets the connection context. Omitted or null keeps the default from the dictionary's metadata.json. See Segmenter
use_mmapboolon when the mmap feature is compiled in (the default)Memory-map the dictionary; only meaningful for filesystem (non-embedded://) dictionaries, and ignored without the mmap feature
max_grouping_leninteger(unbounded)Cap on unknown-word grouping, in characters beyond the first, matching MeCab's max-grouping-size (MeCab defaults to 24). Applied at each position: a run longer than the cap is not grouped there, the single-character candidate (plus the length ladder and dictionary words) remains, and the remaining tail is grouped again once it fits, so no unknown token exceeds cap+1 characters. Omitting the key, or setting 0, leaves grouping unbounded
unknown_word_ladderbooltrueAlso emit the shorter unknown-word candidates up to the LENGTH field in char.def of the character's default category, as MeCab and Vibrato do. false leaves them out, as before v6; other changes since then, such as unknown words that start inside a grouped run, still apply. See Segmenter
break_charactersstring"・"Break characters, each character of the string: no unknown word crosses a boundary between a break character and another character, in every mode, and in decompose mode no system-dictionary word does either (user-dictionary words and words of break characters only stay). An empty string gives MeCab's segmentation, which keeps レノン・ジョン whole while splitting ジョン・レノン. See Break Characters
space_penaltybool or object(the dictionary's rules, if any)Left-space penalty (mecab-ko's left-space-penalty-factor): a candidate that starts right after whitespace and whose first part-of-speech tag is listed gets the cost added. Omitted or null keeps the rules the dictionary ships in its metadata.json (ko-dic ships mecab-ko-dic's, so the penalty is on by default for ko-dic; the other bundled dictionaries ship none); false turns it off; true requires the dictionary's rules (an error when it ships none); an object {"rules": [{"pos": [...], "cost": n}, ...]} gives explicit rules. See Segmenter
% export LINDERA_CONFIG_FILE=./resources/config/lindera.yml

use std::path::PathBuf;

use lindera::analysis::tokenizer::TokenizerBuilder;
use lindera::LinderaResult;

fn main() -> LinderaResult<()> {
    // Load tokenizer configuration from file
    let path = PathBuf::from(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR"))
        .join("../resources")
        .join("config")
        .join("lindera.yml");

    let builder = TokenizerBuilder::from_file(&path)?;

    let tokenizer = builder.build()?;

    let text = "Ｌｉｎｄｅｒａは形態素解析ｴﾝｼﾞﾝです。ユーザー辞書も利用可能です。".to_string();
    println!("text: {text}");

    let tokens = tokenizer.tokenize(&text)?;

    for token in tokens {
        println!(
            "token: {:?}, start: {:?}, end: {:?}, details: {:?}",
            token.surface, token.byte_start, token.byte_end, token.details
        );
    }

    Ok(())
}

Filters

Character filters and token filters are the two pre/post-processing stages of the lindera-analysis Tokenizer pipeline.

  • Character filters transform the input text before segmentation. Byte offsets are corrected automatically so that the resulting tokens still report positions relative to the original, unfiltered text.
  • Token filters transform the list of tokens produced by the segmenter after segmentation.

Both kinds of filters are configured the same way: a kind string (also used with the CLI's --character-filter / --token-filter flags in the form kind:{"json": "args"}) and a JSON args object with filter-specific parameters.

Character Filters

Character filters are configured under the character_filters key of the YAML configuration file. Each entry is applied in order, and each filter's output feeds into the next.

unicode_normalize

Normalizes the input text using one of the four standard Unicode normalization forms.

Parameters:

ArgumentTypeRequiredDescription
kindstringYesOne of nfc, nfd, nfkc, or nfkd

Example:

{
  "kind": "unicode_normalize",
  "args": {
    "kind": "nfkc"
  }
}

japanese_iteration_mark

Normalizes Japanese iteration marks (々, ゝ, ゞ, ヽ, ヾ) by replacing each mark with the character it repeats, adding or removing the voiced sound mark (dakuten) as needed for the hiragana/katakana variants.

Parameters:

ArgumentTypeRequiredDefaultDescription
normalize_kanjiboolNofalseNormalize the kanji iteration mark 々
normalize_kanaboolNofalseNormalize the hiragana/katakana iteration marks ゝ, ゞ, ヽ, ヾ

Example:

{
  "kind": "japanese_iteration_mark",
  "args": {
    "normalize_kanji": true,
    "normalize_kana": true
  }
}

mapping (character filter)

Replaces occurrences of the keys in mapping with their corresponding values, using longest-match search over the input text (built with an Aho-Corasick automaton).

Parameters:

ArgumentTypeRequiredDescription
mappingobject (string to string)YesSubstrings to replace, mapped to their replacements

Example:

{
  "kind": "mapping",
  "args": {
    "mapping": {
      "リンデラ": "Lindera"
    }
  }
}

regex

Replaces every match of a regular expression in the input text with a literal replacement string. Capture groups are not interpolated into the replacement.

Parameters:

ArgumentTypeRequiredDescription
patternstringYesA regular expression (using the regex crate's syntax)
replacementstringYesThe literal string that replaces every match of pattern

Example:

{
  "kind": "regex",
  "args": {
    "pattern": "\\s{2,}",
    "replacement": " "
  }
}

Token Filters

Token filters are configured under the token_filters key of the YAML configuration file. Each filter is applied in order to the token list produced by the segmenter.

japanese_base_form

Replaces the token's surface text with its base (dictionary) form, as registered in the base_form or orthographic_base_form field of the dictionary. Acts as a lemmatizer for verbs and adjectives. Tokens produced by unknown-word processing (token.word_id.is_unknown()) are left unchanged.

This filter takes no configuration parameters.

Example:

{
  "kind": "japanese_base_form"
}

japanese_compound_word

Merges consecutive tokens whose part-of-speech tag matches one of tags into a single compound token.

The merged token's details carry new_tag at the part-of-speech position resolved from the dictionary schema; any leading non-part-of-speech field (SudachiDict's display_surface) and every remaining field are set to *.

Parameters:

ArgumentTypeRequiredDescription
tagsarray<string>YesPart-of-speech tags (up to 4 comma-separated levels) that mark tokens eligible for merging
new_tagstringNoPart-of-speech tag assigned to the merged token. When omitted, the merged token is tagged 複合語

Example:

{
  "kind": "japanese_compound_word",
  "args": {
    "tags": [
      "名詞,数",
      "名詞,接尾,助数詞"
    ],
    "new_tag": "名詞,数"
  }
}

japanese_dependency

Analyzes the dependencies of the text: groups the tokens into bunsetsu (文節), finds the bunsetsu each one depends on, and writes the result on every token. No token is added, removed or changed, so the MeCab and wakati outputs stay as they are; the JSON output gets a dependency key for each token.

The filter is in builds with the dependency feature only: the lindera command and the bindings have it by default, from 7.1.0 on, and the libraries lindera and lindera-analysis do not. A build without it refuses the kind with an error that names the feature. The filter needs a model file of lindera-dependency for the dictionary of the tokenizer; Lindera releases one for IPADIC, which lindera download dependency-ipadic installs, and one for each of unidic, unidic-cwj and unidic-csj (lindera download dependency-unidic and the like). See Token Filter for what is written on a token, how a text is cut into sentences, and how to get or make a model.

Put this filter before any token filter that removes, joins or rewrites tokens: the model reads the tokens as the dictionary gave them. Tokens removed or joined by an earlier filter are refused with an error.

Parameters:

ArgumentTypeRequiredDescription
modelstringYesPath of a model file of lindera-dependency, with a chunker and a parser, for the dictionary of the tokenizer

Example:

{
  "kind": "japanese_dependency",
  "args": {
    "model": "/path/to/ipadic.model"
  }
}

japanese_kana

Converts token text between hiragana and katakana.

Parameters:

ArgumentTypeRequiredDescription
kindstringYes"hiragana" converts katakana to hiragana; "katakana" converts hiragana to katakana

Example:

{
  "kind": "japanese_kana",
  "args": {
    "kind": "hiragana"
  }
}

japanese_katakana_stem

Removes a trailing prolonged sound mark (ー, U+30FC) from katakana tokens, but only when the token is longer than min characters.

Parameters:

ArgumentTypeRequiredDescription
minpositive integerYesMinimum katakana token length (in characters) required before the trailing prolonged sound mark is stemmed

Example:

{
  "kind": "japanese_katakana_stem",
  "args": {
    "min": 3
  }
}

japanese_keep_tags

Keeps only tokens whose part-of-speech tag matches one of tags, removing all others.

Parameters:

ArgumentTypeRequiredDescription
tagsarray<string>YesPart-of-speech tags (up to 4 comma-separated levels) to keep

Example:

{
  "kind": "japanese_keep_tags",
  "args": {
    "tags": [
      "名詞,一般",
      "名詞,固有名詞,一般"
    ]
  }
}

japanese_number

Converts Japanese numeral representations (kanji numerals, formal/legal kanji numerals, and fullwidth digits) in the token's surface text to Arabic numerals.

A token is converted only when every one of its characters takes part in a numeral, the rule Lucene's JapaneseNumberFilter applies. An ordinary word that merely begins with a numeral character is therefore returned unchanged: 一部 stays 一部 rather than becoming 1部.

When this filter follows japanese_compound_word, merge only the 名詞,数 tokens. A counter (名詞,接尾,助数詞) merged into the number token makes the merged token something other than a numeral, so 一万円 is left alone instead of being converted.

Parameters:

ArgumentTypeRequiredDescription
tagsarray<string> or nullNoPart-of-speech tags (up to 4 comma-separated levels) to restrict the conversion to, matched the same way as japanese_keep_tags. When omitted or null, every token is converted

Example:

{
  "kind": "japanese_number",
  "args": {
    "tags": [
      "名詞,数"
    ]
  }
}

japanese_reading_form

Replaces the token's surface text with its reading, in katakana, as registered in the dictionary's reading field. Tokens produced by unknown-word processing (token.word_id.is_unknown()) are left unchanged.

This filter takes no configuration parameters.

Example:

{
  "kind": "japanese_reading_form"
}

japanese_stop_tags

Removes tokens whose part-of-speech tag matches one of tags.

Parameters:

ArgumentTypeRequiredDescription
tagsarray<string>YesPart-of-speech tags (up to 4 comma-separated levels) to remove

Example:

{
  "kind": "japanese_stop_tags",
  "args": {
    "tags": [
      "助詞,格助詞,一般",
      "助詞,係助詞",
      "助詞,連体化",
      "助動詞"
    ]
  }
}

Tags are normalized to exactly four comma-separated levels (missing levels are padded with *) and compared for exact equality against the four part-of-speech details of each token, starting at the field named part_of_speech in the dictionary schema (or at the first detail when the schema has no such field). A bare 助詞 therefore never matches IPADIC particle tokens — they always carry a subcategory such as 助詞,係助詞 — while a bare 助動詞 does match, because auxiliary verbs have no subcategory (助動詞,*,*,*). The same matching rule applies to japanese_keep_tags, japanese_compound_word, and the tags option of japanese_number. Because the position is resolved through the schema, the rule also holds for dictionaries whose schema has leading non-part-of-speech columns, such as SudachiDict's display_surface.

keep_words

Keeps only tokens whose surface text exactly matches one of words.

Parameters:

ArgumentTypeRequiredDescription
wordsarray<string>YesSurface forms to keep

Example:

{
  "kind": "keep_words",
  "args": {
    "words": [
      "すもも",
      "もも"
    ]
  }
}

korean_compound_word

Merges consecutive Korean tokens whose first part-of-speech tag matches one of tags into a single compound token. The merged token keeps the first token's byte_start and position, takes the last token's byte_end, and its position_length is the number of tokens merged. A matching token whose neighbours do not match is left as it is.

ko-dic tokenizes a Sino-Korean numeral into one token per morpheme, so this filter is what turns 이/NR 천/NR 이/NR 십/NR 육/NR back into one token before korean_number converts it:

InputTokens from ko-dicAfter korean_compound_word (tags: ["SN", "NR"], new_tag: "NR")After korean_number
이천이십육년이/NR 천/NR 이/NR 십/NR 육/NR 년/NNBC이천이십육/NR 년/NNBC2026 년
10만10/SN 만/NR10만/NR100000
2천262/SN 천/NR 26/SN2천26/NR2026

Parameters:

ArgumentTypeRequiredDescription
tagsarray<string>YesPart-of-speech tags (the single ko-dic tag, such as NR or SN) that mark tokens eligible for merging
new_tagstringNoPart-of-speech tag assigned to the merged token; its other details are *. When omitted, the merged token is tagged 복합어, which is not a ko-dic tag, so pass a tag such as NR when a following korean_number or korean_keep_tags should pick the merged token up

Example:

{
  "kind": "korean_compound_word",
  "args": {
    "tags": [
      "SN",
      "NR"
    ],
    "new_tag": "NR"
  }
}

With the default settings, ko-dic tags 만 in 만 원 and 십만 원 as the numeral NR, so 십만 원 becomes 십만/NR 원/NNBC. With whitespace skipping turned off (skip_whitespace: false), the word after 만 connects to the whitespace node instead, and ko-dic tags 만 there as the particle JX (만/JX 원/NNG), which stays outside ["SN", "NR"].

korean_decompound

Splits ko-dic compound, inflected and pre-analyzed tokens into the morphemes their expression field lists, reproducing Lucene nori's DecompoundMode. This is the inverse of korean_compound_word, which merges neighbouring tokens. Lindera's Mode::Decompose applies a length penalty tuned for Japanese kanji and does not read these fields, so 무궁화 stays whole in every mode without this filter.

InputTokens from ko-dicmode: "discard"mode: "mixed"
무궁화꽃이무궁화/NNG 꽃/NNG 이/JKS무궁 화 꽃 이무궁화 무궁 화 꽃 이
가곡역가곡역/NNP가곡 역가곡역 가곡 역

Fragment offsets follow nori: only Compound fragments get their own byte range, each covering the text it spells. Inflect and Preanalysis fragments share the whole token's span, because an inflected form's fragments need not be substrings of it (갔 decomposes to 가 + 았).

A Compound token is carved only when its fragments spell its surface exactly; otherwise it shares its span too. That covers the 12 bundled ko-dic entries whose fragments are not the surface's own text (안지랑역 = 안지 + 역, 고춧값 = 고추 + 값), where nori's offsets point some fragments at text they do not spell, as well as a user-dictionary entry such as 프린터3D = 프린터 + 쓰리디 and a surface an earlier filter has rewritten. For every other bundled entry the offsets are nori's, and every offset is safe to slice the text with.

In discard the fragments take consecutive positions starting at the compound's own; in mixed the compound keeps that position with a position_length spanning its fragments, which are then emitted from the same position onward. Tokens after the expansion shift by the positions it added, and only by those, so a gap left by an earlier filter such as korean_stop_tags survives.

Only tokens spanning a single position are expanded, so the compound a mixed pass keeps is not split again. Put the filter in a chain once all the same: a single-fragment entry kept by mixed still spans one position. When combining it with korean_compound_word, place the merge first; merging never joins tokens that overlap in byte range, so the reverse order does not corrupt anything, but merging first lets it see the segmenter's own tokens.

A fragment takes its own part-of-speech tag and semantic class and blanks the fields that describe the compound (type, expression, first_part_of_speech, last_part_of_speech, reading, presence_absence). Blanking the reading matches nori, whose DecompoundToken.getReading() returns null; korean_reading_form skips *, so a fragment keeps its own surface.

Applied to a dictionary whose schema has no type/expression fields, the filter warns once per configured filter and passes every token through unchanged.

Parameters:

ArgumentTypeRequiredDescription
modestringNo"discard" (default, as in nori) replaces the compound with its fragments; "mixed" keeps the compound and emits the fragments as well
typesarray<string>NoThe type values to decompound, case-sensitive. Defaults to ["Compound", "Inflect", "Preanalysis"]; an empty list or any other value is rejected

Example:

{
  "kind": "korean_decompound",
  "args": {
    "mode": "discard",
    "types": [
      "Compound",
      "Inflect",
      "Preanalysis"
    ]
  }
}

korean_keep_tags

Keeps only Korean tokens whose first part-of-speech tag matches one of tags.

Parameters:

ArgumentTypeRequiredDescription
tagsarray<string>YesPart-of-speech tags to keep

Example:

{
  "kind": "korean_keep_tags",
  "args": {
    "tags": [
      "NNG"
    ]
  }
}

korean_number

Converts Sino-Korean numeral representations (Hangul numerals, Hanja numerals, and fullwidth digits) in the token's surface text to Arabic numerals. Native Korean numerals (하나, 둘, 열, 스물, ...) have no positional structure and are left unchanged.

Each token is converted on its own. ko-dic tokenizes a Sino-Korean numeral into one token per morpheme, so the tokens of a single number do not add up to one Arabic numeral:

InputTokens from ko-dicAfter korean_number
이천이십육년이/NR 천/NR 이/NR 십/NR 육/NR 년/NNBC2 1000 2 10 6 년
10만10/SN 만/NR10 10000

Put korean_compound_word in front of this filter to merge those tokens first, the way japanese_compound_word does for IPADIC. Its new_tag must be one of this filter's tags for the merged token to be converted:

[
  {"kind": "korean_compound_word", "args": {"tags": ["SN", "NR"], "new_tag": "NR"}},
  {"kind": "korean_number", "args": {"tags": ["SN", "NR"]}}
]

With that chain 이천이십육년 becomes 2026 년, 10만 becomes 100000 and 2천26 becomes 2026. A single token that holds the whole numeral, such as the Hanja 二千二十六/SH, is converted in full by this filter alone.

Parameters:

ArgumentTypeRequiredDescription
tagsarray<string> or nullNoPart-of-speech tags to restrict the conversion to. Omitted, it defaults to ["SN", "NR"]; null converts every token

A token is converted only when every one of its characters is a numeral, the rule Lucene's KoreanNumberFilter applies. That is what keeps native Korean numerals intact: 일곱 ("seven") starts with the Sino-Korean 일, and a character-by-character conversion would give 1곱.

Hangul numerals are also homographs of very common morphemes (이 is a subject particle, 만 an auxiliary particle), and those are single characters that the all-numeral rule cannot separate from a numeral. That is why the default is restricted to the numeral tags.

Add SH to convert Hanja numerals as well. The coverage is partial in two ways: ko-dic tags whole Hanja words as NNG (參加, 萬歲 are untouched), while a single Hanja character it cannot attach to a word is SH on its own, so 十字架 becomes 10 字 架 and 百貨店 becomes 100 貨 店.

Example:

{
  "kind": "korean_number",
  "args": {
    "tags": [
      "SN",
      "NR"
    ]
  }
}

korean_reading_form

Replaces the token's surface text with its reading, as registered in the dictionary's reading field. Tokens produced by unknown-word processing (token.word_id.is_unknown()) are left unchanged.

This filter takes no configuration parameters.

Example:

{
  "kind": "korean_reading_form"
}

korean_stop_tags

Removes Korean tokens whose first part-of-speech tag matches one of tags.

Parameters:

ArgumentTypeRequiredDescription
tagsarray<string>YesPart-of-speech tags to remove

Example:

{
  "kind": "korean_stop_tags",
  "args": {
    "tags": [
      "EP",
      "EF",
      "JKG"
    ]
  }
}

length

Keeps only tokens whose surface text length (in characters) falls within [min, max].

Parameters:

ArgumentTypeRequiredDescription
minunsigned integerNoMinimum character length (inclusive)
maxunsigned integerNoMaximum character length (inclusive)

Example:

{
  "kind": "length",
  "args": {
    "min": 2,
    "max": 3
  }
}

lowercase

Converts token surface text to lowercase.

This filter takes no configuration parameters.

Example:

{
  "kind": "lowercase"
}

mapping (token filter)

Replaces occurrences of the keys in mapping with their corresponding values in each token's surface text, using longest-match search (built with an Aho-Corasick automaton). This is the token-level counterpart of the mapping character filter.

Parameters:

ArgumentTypeRequiredDescription
mappingobject (string to string)YesSubstrings to replace, mapped to their replacements

Example:

{
  "kind": "mapping",
  "args": {
    "mapping": {
      "籠": "篭"
    }
  }
}

remove_diacritical_mark

Removes diacritical (combining) marks from token surface text, re-applying the text's original Unicode normalization form afterward.

Parameters:

ArgumentTypeRequiredDefaultDescription
japaneseboolNofalseAlso remove Japanese (han-)dakuten combining marks (e.g. from decomposed voiced/semi-voiced kana)

Example:

{
  "kind": "remove_diacritical_mark",
  "args": {
    "japanese": false
  }
}

stop_words

Removes tokens whose surface text exactly matches one of words.

Parameters:

ArgumentTypeRequiredDescription
wordsarray<string>YesSurface forms to remove

Example:

{
  "kind": "stop_words",
  "args": {
    "words": [
      "も",
      "の"
    ]
  }
}

uppercase

Converts token surface text to uppercase.

This filter takes no configuration parameters.

Example:

{
  "kind": "uppercase"
}

YAML Configuration

Character filters and token filters are configured together with the segmenter in a single YAML file. See Configuration for the full file format; the relevant excerpt looks like this:

character_filters:
  - kind: "unicode_normalize"
    args:
      kind: "nfkc"
  - kind: "japanese_iteration_mark"
    args:
      normalize_kanji: true
      normalize_kana: true

token_filters:
  - kind: "japanese_stop_tags"
    args:
      tags:
        - "助詞,格助詞,一般"
        - "助詞,係助詞"
        - "助詞,連体化"
        - "助動詞"
  - kind: "japanese_katakana_stem"
    args:
      min: 3
  - kind: "lowercase"
  - kind: "length"
    args:
      min: 2

Rust API

Character filters and token filters can also be created and applied programmatically:

use lindera::dictionary::load_dictionary;
use lindera::mode::Mode;
use lindera::segmenter::Segmenter;
use lindera::analysis::character_filter::BoxCharacterFilter;
use lindera::analysis::character_filter::unicode_normalize::{
    UnicodeNormalizeCharacterFilter, UnicodeNormalizeKind,
};
use lindera::analysis::token_filter::BoxTokenFilter;
use lindera::analysis::token_filter::japanese_stop_tags::JapaneseStopTagsTokenFilter;
use lindera::analysis::token_filter::japanese_katakana_stem::JapaneseKatakanaStemTokenFilter;
use lindera::analysis::tokenizer::Tokenizer;
use lindera::LinderaResult;

fn main() -> LinderaResult<()> {
    let dictionary = load_dictionary("embedded://ipadic")?;
    let segmenter = Segmenter::new(Mode::Normal, dictionary, None);

    let mut tokenizer = Tokenizer::new(segmenter);

    // Add a character filter
    let normalize_filter = UnicodeNormalizeCharacterFilter::new(UnicodeNormalizeKind::NFKC);
    tokenizer.append_character_filter(BoxCharacterFilter::from(normalize_filter));

    // Add token filters
    let stop_tags_filter = JapaneseStopTagsTokenFilter::new(
        vec![
            "助詞,格助詞,一般".to_string(),
            "助詞,係助詞".to_string(),
            "助詞,連体化".to_string(),
            "助動詞".to_string(),
        ]
        .into_iter()
        .collect(),
    );
    tokenizer.append_token_filter(BoxTokenFilter::from(stop_tags_filter));

    let katakana_stem_filter =
        JapaneseKatakanaStemTokenFilter::new(std::num::NonZeroUsize::new(3).unwrap());
    tokenizer.append_token_filter(BoxTokenFilter::from(katakana_stem_filter));

    // Tokenize with filters applied
    let tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Linderaは形態素解析エンジンです。")?;

    for token in tokens {
        println!(
            "token: {:?}, details: {:?}",
            token.surface, token.details
        );
    }

    Ok(())
}

The append_character_filter and append_token_filter methods add filters in order. Character filters are applied sequentially to the text before segmentation; token filters are applied sequentially to the token list after segmentation.

Architecture

Key Components

CharacterFilter

A trait for filters that preprocess text before segmentation. Each implementation provides a name() and an apply(&self, text: &mut String) -> LinderaResult<OffsetMapping> method that rewrites text in place and returns an OffsetMapping describing every transformation it performed.

The OffsetMapping (built from a list of Transformation records) lets the Tokenizer translate token byte offsets computed against the filtered text back to byte offsets in the original input, even after multiple filters have run in sequence. BoxCharacterFilter wraps any CharacterFilter implementation as a boxed, cloneable trait object, and CharacterFilterLoader builds one from a kind string plus a serde_json::Value of arguments (used both by YAML configuration loading and by CLI flag parsing).

TokenFilter

A trait for filters that post-process the tokens produced by the segmenter. Each implementation provides a name() and an apply(&self, tokens: &mut Vec<Token<'_>>) -> LinderaResult<()> method that modifies, merges, reorders, or removes tokens in place. BoxTokenFilter wraps any TokenFilter implementation as a boxed, cloneable trait object, and TokenFilterLoader builds one from a kind string plus a serde_json::Value of arguments, mirroring CharacterFilterLoader.

Tokenizer / TokenizerBuilder

Tokenizer composes character filters, a lindera::segmenter::Segmenter, and token filters into a single analysis pipeline. Calling tokenize runs the character filters over the input text, segments the filtered text, applies the token filters to the resulting tokens, and finally corrects each token's byte offsets back to the original text via the recorded OffsetMappings.

TokenizerBuilder assembles a Tokenizer from a TokenizerConfig (a serde_json::Value), which can be constructed programmatically, loaded from a YAML file (via TokenizerBuilder::from_file, or automatically from the LINDERA_CONFIG_FILE environment variable via TokenizerBuilder::new), or built up incrementally with set_segmenter_mode, set_segmenter_dictionary, append_character_filter, and append_token_filter. See Configuration for the YAML file format and Filters for the full filter reference.

TokenizerBuilder::build loads the dictionaries the configuration names. TokenizerBuilder::build_with_dictionaries (and Tokenizer::from_config_with_dictionaries) takes already-loaded dictionaries instead, such as ones loaded from bytes, and applies every other setting of the configuration to them, filters included; see Building from Config for how the given dictionaries replace the configured ones. The WASM binding's TokenizerBuilder builds its tokenizers this way, with the dictionaries set by setDictionaryInstance() and setUserDictionaryInstance().

AnalysisWorker

AnalysisWorker (created with Tokenizer::new_worker or Tokenizer::into_worker) is a reusable session over the full analysis chain. It owns every per-call buffer — the Viterbi lattice and backtrace scratch (via SegmentWorker), the normalized-text buffer the character filters operate on, and the offset-mapping scratch — so repeated tokenize calls avoid the per-call allocations Tokenizer::tokenize pays. When character filters are configured, token surfaces borrow the worker's buffer instead of being copied into per-token Strings. Returned tokens borrow the worker and must be consumed before the next call; for multi-threaded use, create one worker per thread (or guard one with a Mutex, as lindera-binding does), or tokenize a list of texts with an AnalysisWorkerPool. See the Segmenter page for the underlying SegmentWorker and its automatic memory-shrink policy.

AnalysisWorker's public methods:

  • tokenize(&mut self, text: &str) — tokenizes text through the full analysis chain, reusing the worker's internal buffers; produces exactly the same tokens as Tokenizer::tokenize.
  • tokenize_nbest(&mut self, text: &str, n, unique, cost_threshold) — tokenizes text and returns the top-N results with costs, reusing the worker's internal buffers; produces exactly the same results as Tokenizer::tokenize_nbest.
  • set_mode(&mut self, mode: Mode) — sets the segmentation mode for subsequent calls.
  • set_keep_whitespace(&mut self, keep: bool) — sets whether whitespace tokens are kept in the output for subsequent calls; kept whitespace also stays in the lattice, so the other tokens can differ.
  • set_skip_whitespace(&mut self, skip: bool) — sets whether whitespace is skipped in the lattice for subsequent calls when whitespace tokens are not kept (by default the dictionary's setting).
  • set_max_grouping_len(&mut self, max_grouping_len: Option<usize>), set_unknown_word_ladder(&mut self, unknown_word_ladder: bool) — set the unknown-word grouping cap and the length ladder for subsequent calls.
  • set_break_characters(&mut self, chars: &str) — sets the break characters for subsequent calls (・ by default; an empty string gives MeCab's segmentation).
  • set_space_penalty(&mut self, space_penalty: Option<SpacePenaltyConfig>), set_space_penalty_from_dictionary(&mut self) — set the left-space penalty rules for subsequent calls, or restore the dictionary's.
  • shrink_to(&mut self, text_len_hint: usize) — immediately shrinks the worker's internal buffers to what an input of text_len_hint bytes needs.
  • reset(&mut self) — discards all internal buffers, replacing them with fresh ones; intended for recovery paths (e.g. after a panic poisoned a mutex holding the worker), with configuration (dictionary, filters, mode) preserved.
  • to_tokenizer(&self) — returns a Tokenizer with the worker's configuration, the settings changed by the setters above included, from which more workers that tokenize as this one does can be made. The user dictionary, if any, is copied.

AnalysisWorkerPool

AnalysisWorkerPool (created with Tokenizer::new_worker_pool or Tokenizer::into_worker_pool) tokenizes a list of texts on several threads. Every text is tokenized as a call of its own, as AnalysisWorker::tokenize tokenizes it, and the results come back in the order of the texts, so they are the same for every number of threads. A list of the lines of a document gives the tokens that lindera tokenize gives, since it also tokenizes every line on its own; it does not give those of the whole document as one text, whose offsets, positions and N-best results span its lines.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::num::NonZeroUsize;

let mut pool = tokenizer.into_worker_pool();
let threads = std::thread::available_parallelism().unwrap_or(NonZeroUsize::MIN);
let surfaces: Vec<Vec<String>> = pool.tokenize_batch(&lines, threads, |tokens| {
    tokens.into_iter().map(|token| token.surface.into_owned()).collect()
})?;
}

The closure runs on the thread that tokenized the text, right after it: the tokens borrow that thread's worker, so it turns them into what the caller keeps (Strings, counts, a formatted output), and that work runs in parallel too.

  • tokenize_batch(&mut self, texts, max_threads, f) — tokenizes every text on up to max_threads threads, the calling thread included, and returns the results of f in the order of texts.
  • tokenize_nbest_batch(&mut self, texts, n, unique, cost_threshold, max_threads, f) — the same with AnalysisWorker::tokenize_nbest; f gets the (tokens, cost) pairs of one text.
  • worker_count(&self), truncate_workers(&mut self, max_workers) — the number of workers the pool holds, and dropping the ones beyond max_workers.
  • shrink_to(&mut self, text_len_hint), reset(&mut self) — as AnalysisWorker's, for every worker.

How a batch runs:

  • The pool starts with one worker and makes more from it (to_tokenizer) when a batch runs on more threads than it has workers. Every worker keeps its buffers for the next batches and holds its own copy of the user dictionary, if any; the system dictionary is shared.
  • A batch runs on the calling thread alone when it is given one thread, one text or a short input (the input of a thread is at least 16 KiB), and always on wasm, which has no threads. Otherwise it starts threads with std::thread::scope, which hand out the texts in chunks.
  • If texts fail, the error of the first one in input order is returned, as a loop over the texts would return it, and the texts after it may not be tokenized. A panic, in the tokenization or in f, is resumed on the calling thread in the same way, after the worker that panicked is reset, so the pool stays usable.
  • The workers are clones of one tokenizer, so a filter of your own whose instances keep state of their own gives each worker its own state.

API Reference

The API reference is available. Please see following URL:

  • lindera-analysis

Lindera Dependency

Lindera Dependency (lindera-dependency) is a crate for Japanese bunsetsu dependency analysis: it groups the morphemes of a sentence into bunsetsu (文節) and finds, for each bunsetsu, the bunsetsu it depends on.

彼は 本を 読んだ。
彼は ──────┐
本を ──────┤
読んだ。 ◀──┘   (root)

Status

The crate is on crates.io from Lindera 7.1.0 on, and each release of Lindera publishes the models for IPADIC and for the three UniDic dictionaries with it. The analysis is complete from morphemes to dependencies: the training data, the chunker, the parser, the model file, the evaluation and a command for text are here, and the token filter of Lindera is in the default builds of the lindera command and of the bindings.

Start with the Installation and the Quick Start. The work is tracked in #1417.

What it can do

  • Segment the morphemes of a sentence into bunsetsu (chunking), with a conditional random field and a model that is a table of weights. With IPADIC, the F-score is 96.85 on the dev file and 96.92 on the test file of UD Japanese-GSD.
  • Keep a model in one file per dictionary and read it in place: from bytes embedded in a program, read from a file or mapped into memory, without copying its tables. The file names its dictionary, and morphemes that cannot be of that dictionary are refused.
  • Parse the dependencies of the bunsetsu with shift-reduce and a classifier over features and pairs of features, as CaboCha and J.DepP do, and train that classifier. With IPADIC, 90.11% of the bunsetsu of the dev file of UD Japanese-GSD get the right head with the bunsetsu of the answer (88.53% on the test file), and 85.39% from the morphemes (84.47%).
  • Parse plain text from the command line, tokenized with a Lindera dictionary, and write what cabocha -f1 writes.
  • Run as a token filter of Lindera, japanese_dependency: from the lindera command, a configuration file, Rust and the five bindings, with the bunsetsu and the head of each token in the JSON output and on the Token.
  • Give the head word and the function word of a bunsetsu, and recognize punctuation and brackets, from a schema of the dictionary. IPADIC is the first schema.
  • Read and write the lattice format of CaboCha (cabocha -f1), and check that a sentence is the tree the parsers assume.
  • Make training data from a dependency corpus such as UD Japanese-GSD, on the morphemes of the dictionary the parser will run with.
  • Convert the model CaboCha distributes for IPA into a model file that analyzes as CaboCha does. Such a model is limited to research and personal use, as CaboCha's.
  • Evaluate chunking and dependency accuracy as CaboCha and J.DepP count them, and compare two outputs with a paired test.

The default build has no dependency and builds for wasm32-unknown-unknown: it holds the types, the lattice format, the schema, the model file, the chunker and the parser. The command is behind the cli feature, and the training and the evaluation behind the train feature.

For the decisions behind the crate and the numbers they rest on, see the design notes.

Installation

lindera-dependency is on crates.io from Lindera 7.1.0 on. Most programs do not depend on it directly: they use the token filter japanese_dependency of the Lindera tokenizer, which the lindera crate, the lindera command and the bindings carry.

In a tokenizer

The filter is behind the dependency feature of lindera:

[dependencies]
lindera = { version = "7.1", features = ["dependency"] }

The lindera command and the bindings (Python, Node.js, Ruby, PHP, WebAssembly) have the feature in their default builds, from 7.1.0 on: the packages you install have the filter. See Token Filter, and the installation page of each: command, Python, Node.js, Ruby, PHP, WebAssembly.

A build of the command without the default features knows the name of the filter and says what is missing:

Error: LinderaError { kind: FeatureDisabled, source: the token filter japanese_dependency needs a build with the feature `dependency` }

The crate

[dependencies]
lindera-dependency = "7.1"

The default build has no dependency and builds for wasm32-unknown-unknown: it takes any sequence of morphemes, from Lindera or not. The feature flags add the command, the training and the embedded model.

The lindera-dependency command, which parses plain text and writes the lattice format, is behind cli:

cargo install lindera-dependency --features cli

The model

The analysis needs a model file for the dictionary of the tokenizer. Lindera publishes four with each release: one for IPADIC (The model for IPADIC) and one for each of unidic, unidic-cwj and unidic-csj (The models for UniDic). A model is not part of a package or of a crate, as the dictionaries are not. There are three ways to get one, shown here for IPADIC; for a UniDic dictionary, its name takes the place of ipadic:

  • lindera download dependency-ipadic installs the model of the version of the command, and prints the path of the model file (download).
  • lindera-dependency-ipadic-<version>.zip, on the page of a release, holds the model file dependency.model and its NOTICE.txt.
  • The feature embed-dependency-ipadic of lindera, of the command and of the bindings (embed-model-ipadic of lindera-dependency) embeds it in the build (Embedding it).

The model is under the MIT license, and comes with a notice (License of the model).

Quick Start

This page parses one sentence with the model that Lindera releases, from the command line and from Rust. It needs Lindera 7.1.0 or later.

Getting the dictionary and the model

The model for IPADIC goes with the IPADIC dictionary. lindera download installs both, and prints the path to pass on:

% lindera download ipadic
/home/user/.local/share/lindera/dictionaries/ipadic
% lindera download dependency-ipadic
/home/user/.local/share/lindera/dictionaries/dependency-ipadic/dependency.model

The first is the directory of the dictionary, the second the model file. $(lindera download <name>) gives each to a script.

With the lindera command

The token filter japanese_dependency writes on every token its bunsetsu and the bunsetsu that one depends on:

% DICT=$(lindera download ipadic)
% MODEL=$(lindera download dependency-ipadic)
% echo "彼は赤い花を見た。" | lindera tokenize --dict "$DICT" --output json \
    --token-filter "japanese_dependency:{\"model\":\"$MODEL\"}"

Each token of the JSON output has a dependency. The surface of each token with the bunsetsu, the head and the role of its dependency:

Tokenbunsetsuheadrole
彼03head
は03function
赤い12head_function
花23head
を23function
見3nullhead
た3nullfunction
。3nullother

The sentence has four bunsetsu: 彼は (0) and 花を (2) depend on 見た。 (3), 赤い (1) on 花を, and the last one on nothing. Token Filter describes the fields, how a text is cut into sentences, and the same from a configuration file and from the bindings.

With the lindera-dependency command

The command of the crate writes the lattice format, which is what cabocha -f1 writes:

% cargo install lindera-dependency --features cli
% echo "彼は赤い花を見た。" | lindera-dependency parse --model "$MODEL" --dict "$DICT"

* 0 3D 0/1 0.000000
彼	名詞,代名詞,一般,*,*,*,彼,カレ,カレ
は	助詞,係助詞,*,*,*,*,は,ハ,ワ
* 1 2D 0/0 0.704616
赤い	形容詞,自立,*,*,形容詞・アウオ段,基本形,赤い,アカイ,アカイ
* 2 3D 0/1 0.000000
花	名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,花,ハナ,ハナ
を	助詞,格助詞,一般,*,*,*,を,ヲ,ヲ
* 3 -1D 0/1 0.000000
見	動詞,自立,*,*,一段,連用形,見る,ミ,ミ
た	助動詞,*,*,*,特殊・タ,基本形,た,タ,タ
。	記号,句点,*,*,*,*,。,。,。
EOS

A line * 1 2D 0/0 0.704616 starts a bunsetsu: its number, the number of the bunsetsu it depends on, its head word and function word, and the score of the decision. See Command Line.

From Rust

[dependencies]
lindera = { version = "7.1", features = ["dependency"] }

use std::path::Path;

use lindera::analysis::token_filter::BoxTokenFilter;
use lindera::analysis::token_filter::japanese_dependency::JapaneseDependencyTokenFilter;
use lindera::analysis::tokenizer::Tokenizer;
use lindera::dictionary::load_dictionary;
use lindera::mode::Mode;
use lindera::segmenter::Segmenter;

fn main() -> lindera::LinderaResult<()> {
    // The paths that `lindera download ipadic` and
    // `lindera download dependency-ipadic` print.
    let mut args = std::env::args().skip(1);
    let dictionary = args.next().expect("the directory of the dictionary");
    let model = args.next().expect("the model file");

    let dictionary = load_dictionary(&dictionary)?;
    let mut tokenizer = Tokenizer::new(Segmenter::new(Mode::Normal, dictionary, None));
    let filter = JapaneseDependencyTokenFilter::from_path(Path::new(&model))?;
    tokenizer.append_token_filter(BoxTokenFilter::from(filter));

    for token in tokenizer.tokenize("彼は赤い花を見た。")? {
        if let Some(dependency) = token.dependency() {
            // The bunsetsu of the token, and the bunsetsu that one depends on.
            println!(
                "{}\t{}\t{:?}\t{}",
                token.surface,
                dependency.bunsetsu,
                dependency.head,
                dependency.role.as_str()
            );
        }
    }
    Ok(())
}

With the two paths as its arguments, it prints:

彼	0	Some(3)	head
は	0	Some(3)	function
赤い	1	Some(2)	head_function
花	2	Some(3)	head
を	2	Some(3)	function
見	3	None	head
た	3	None	function
。	3	None	other

To parse morphemes that do not come from Lindera, or to use the chunker and the parser on their own, see Parsing and Model File.

Architecture

Module Structure

lindera-dependency/src/
├── lib.rs                # Public API re-exports
├── morpheme.rs           # Morpheme trait, DictionaryMorpheme
├── sentence.rs           # Sentence, Bunsetsu, ArcType, Violation
├── lattice.rs            # Reading and writing the lattice format of CaboCha
├── schema.rs             # Schema: columns, head word and function word
├── schema/
│   ├── pattern.rs        # Pattern over the morphemes of a bunsetsu
│   ├── symbols.rs        # Marks, Symbols, SurfaceRule: punctuation and brackets
│   └── normalization.rs  # Normalization: a table that replaces parts of a surface
├── chunker.rs            # Chunker
├── chunker/
│   ├── columns.rs        # Column: what a template reads from a morpheme
│   ├── template.rs       # Template in the format of CRF++
│   ├── model.rs          # ChunkerData, ChunkerModel: the table of weights
│   ├── decode.rs         # Viterbi over the two labels
│   └── train.rs          # Training with lindera-crf (train)
├── model.rs              # Model, ModelBuilder: the model file of a dictionary
├── model/
│   └── table.rs          # A table from strings to values, read in place
├── parser.rs             # Parser
├── parser/
│   ├── features.rs       # Group, FeatureSet: the features of a decision
│   ├── shift_reduce.rs   # The loop over the bunsetsu
│   ├── classifier.rs     # Classifier, LinearClassifier
│   ├── model.rs          # ParserModel, ParserPart: the weights, in memory and on a file
│   ├── train.rs          # Training: dual coordinate descent, passive-aggressive (train)
│   └── oracle.rs         # Training instances from an answer
├── corpus.rs             # Training data from a dependency corpus (train)
├── corpus/
│   ├── conllu.rs         # Reading CoNLL-U
│   ├── convert.rs        # Word dependencies to bunsetsu dependencies
│   └── project.rs        # Bunsetsu onto the morphemes of a dictionary
├── evaluation.rs         # Chunking and dependency accuracy (train)

├── cabocha/
│   ├── crfpp.rs          # Reading a CRF++ model in text

│   └── normalizer.rule   # CaboCha's table for the normalization of a surface
├── error.rs              # Error types
├── bytes.rs              # Helpers for the bytes of a model
└── bin/
    ├── lindera-dependency.rs   # The command: parse, chunk (cli)
    └── lindera-dependency/
        └── train.rs            # The subcommands of training and evaluation (train)

Key Components

Morpheme

A morpheme is a surface and the feature columns of its dictionary. Morpheme is a trait, so the crate depends on no tokenizer and a type of your own can be analyzed:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use lindera_dependency::Morpheme;

struct Word {
    surface: &'static str,
    features: [&'static str; 2],
}

impl Morpheme for Word {
    fn surface(&self) -> &str {
        self.surface
    }

    fn feature(&self, index: usize) -> Option<&str> {
        self.features.get(index).copied()
    }
}

let word = Word { surface: "本", features: ["名詞", "一般"] };
assert_eq!(word.feature(1), Some("一般"));
assert_eq!(word.features(), "名詞,一般");
}

What a column means depends on the dictionary: in IPADIC, column 0 is the part of speech and column 6 the base form. The crate reads columns by role through a schema, not by number.

Sentence / Bunsetsu

A Sentence holds its morphemes and the Bunsetsu that group them. A bunsetsu is a range of morphemes with:

  • its head: the index of the bunsetsu it depends on, or None for the root;
  • the type of the arc to the head (ArcType): D for a plain dependency, P for coordination, A for apposition, I for incomplete coordination;
  • optionally the positions of its head word and of its function word, and a score.

Sentence::violations reports the ways a sentence is not the tree the parsers assume: one root that is the last bunsetsu, every head to the right of its bunsetsu, and no crossing arcs.

The lattice format

The lattice module reads and writes the format of cabocha -f1, which the tools of CaboCha and of J.DepP exchange. A bunsetsu line starts with *: the id of the bunsetsu, the id of its head followed by the arc type (-1 for the root), then optionally the positions of the head word and the function word and a score. A morpheme line is the surface, a tab and the feature string. EOS ends a sentence.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use lindera_dependency::Morpheme;
use lindera_dependency::lattice;

// 彼は | 本を | 読んだ。 as `cabocha -f1` writes it.
let text = "\
* 0 2D 0/1 -1.500000
彼\t名詞,代名詞,一般,*,*,*,彼,カレ,カレ
は\t助詞,係助詞,*,*,*,*,は,ハ,ワ
* 1 2D 0/1 -1.500000
本\t名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,本,ホン,ホン
を\t助詞,格助詞,一般,*,*,*,を,ヲ,ヲ
* 2 -1D 0/1 0.000000
読ん\t動詞,自立,*,*,五段・マ行,連用タ接続,読む,ヨン,ヨン
だ\t助動詞,*,*,*,特殊・タ,基本形,だ,ダ,ダ
。\t記号,句点,*,*,*,*,。,。,。
EOS
";
let sentences = lattice::parse(text)?;
let sentence = &sentences[0];
for bunsetsu in &sentence.bunsetsu {
    let surface: String = sentence.morphemes[bunsetsu.morphemes.clone()]
        .iter()
        .map(|morpheme| morpheme.surface())
        .collect();
    println!("{surface} -> {:?} ({})", bunsetsu.head, bunsetsu.arc_type);
}
assert!(sentence.violations().is_empty());

// Writing gives the text back.
let mut output = Vec::new();
lattice::write(&mut output, sentence)?;
assert_eq!(output, text.as_bytes());
}
彼は -> Some(2) (D)
本を -> Some(2) (D)
読んだ。 -> None (D)

A sentence without bunsetsu lines is a sentence of morphemes only, as a tokenizer writes it in the MeCab format. A score is written with six decimals, as CaboCha writes it.

Schema

A Schema holds what is known about a dictionary as data: which columns hold the part of speech, the conjugation and the base form, which morphemes are function words and which are particles, and how symbols are recognized. See Head and Function Word.

Chunker / ChunkerModel

A Chunker segments morphemes into bunsetsu with a table from feature string to weights, and with the schema, the columns and the template the table was trained with. It reads them through the ChunkerData trait: from a ChunkerModel in memory, which is what training gives, or from the chunker part of a model file. See Chunking.

Model / ModelBuilder

A Model is the model file of a dictionary, read in place from bytes it owns or borrows: the name of the dictionary, its schema, and the trained parts, the chunker and the parser. Model::analyze takes a sentence from morphemes to dependencies. ModelBuilder writes a file. See Model File.

Parser / Classifier

A Parser finds the head of each bunsetsu with shift-reduce. The features of a decision are strings made through the schema; a FeatureSet says which groups of them are made; a Classifier scores them, by adding the weights of the features and of their pairs. The classifier of a model file is a ParserPart, which reads the weights on the bytes of the file; ParserModel holds them in memory, as training gives them; LinearClassifier takes weights made by hand. parser::instances gives the training instances from a sentence with its answer, and parser::train trains on them. See Parsing.

The command

With the cli feature the crate builds the lindera-dependency command, which tokenizes with lindera-segmenter and has no training code. The train feature adds the subcommands that make training data, train and evaluate:

SubcommandFeatureWhat it doesPage
parsecliParses plain text, or input that is tokenized or segmented already, and writes the lattice formatCommand Line
chunkcliSegments the morphemes of a file again with a model fileChunking
converttrainMakes training data from a CoNLL-U file with bunsetsu labelsTraining Data
evaluatetrainCompares an output with the answerEvaluation
splittrainWrites the folds of a cross-validationEvaluation
train-chunkertrainTrains the chunker and writes a model fileChunking
instancestrainWrites the training instances of the parserParsing
train-parsertrainTrains the parser and writes a model file, with the chunker of another oneParsing
convert-cabochatrainConverts the chunker and parser models of CaboCha into a model fileCaboCha's Models

The command is in this crate, not in lindera-cli: it writes the lattice format and holds the training, which a user of the tokenizer does not need. lindera-cli runs the parser as a token filter.

Feature Flags

FeatureDescriptionDefault
(none)The types, the lattice format, the schema, the model file, the chunker and the parser. No dependency; builds for wasm32-unknown-unknownYes
cliThe lindera-dependency command with parse and chunk, which tokenizes with lindera-segmenter. No training codeNo
trainThe corpus and evaluation modules, the training of the chunker with lindera-crf and of the parser, and their subcommands (implies cli)No
embed-ipadicEmbeds IPADIC in the command, for --dict embedded://ipadic (implies cli)No
embed-model-ipadicEmbeds the model for IPADIC, for embedded::model("ipadic") and --model embedded://ipadic. A build dependency, and none of the libraryNo
embed-model-unidic, embed-model-unidic-cwj, embed-model-unidic-csjEmbed the models for UniDic, for embedded::model("unidic") and --model embedded://unidic, and the same with the two other namesNo

The crate depends on lindera-segmenter at most, never on lindera or lindera-analysis: the token filter makes lindera-analysis depend on this crate, behind its dependency feature.

Chunking

The chunker segments the morphemes of a sentence into bunsetsu. It decides, for every morpheme, whether it starts a bunsetsu (B) or continues one (I), with a conditional random field over the two labels, as CaboCha does.

Chunking is in the default build and needs no other crate: the model is a table from feature string to the weights of B and I, with the weights of the transitions, and the labels are found by Viterbi. The table is read where it is in a model file. Training is behind the train feature.

Chunking a sentence

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use lindera_dependency::lattice::{self, LatticeMorpheme};
use lindera_dependency::model::Model;
use lindera_dependency::{Bunsetsu, Morpheme, Sentence};

let model = Model::new(std::fs::read("chunker.model")?)?;
let chunker = model.chunker().expect("the file has a chunker");

// The morphemes of 彼は本を読んだ。 as IPADIC gives them. Any type that
// implements `Morpheme` will do.
let morphemes = vec![
    LatticeMorpheme::new("彼", "名詞,代名詞,一般,*,*,*,彼,カレ,カレ"),
    LatticeMorpheme::new("は", "助詞,係助詞,*,*,*,*,は,ハ,ワ"),
    LatticeMorpheme::new("本", "名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,本,ホン,ホン"),
    LatticeMorpheme::new("を", "助詞,格助詞,一般,*,*,*,を,ヲ,ヲ"),
    LatticeMorpheme::new("読ん", "動詞,自立,*,*,五段・マ行,連用タ接続,読む,ヨン,ヨン"),
    LatticeMorpheme::new("だ", "助動詞,*,*,*,特殊・タ,基本形,だ,ダ,ダ"),
    LatticeMorpheme::new("。", "記号,句点,*,*,*,*,。,。,。"),
];

// The ranges of the bunsetsu, as indices into the morphemes.
let ranges = chunker.chunk(&morphemes)?;
assert_eq!(ranges, [0..2, 2..4, 4..7]);
}

Chunker::chunk takes &self, and a chunker is Send + Sync, so one chunker serves several threads. The first morpheme always starts a bunsetsu, and an empty sentence has none.

The morphemes have to come from the dictionary the model was trained with, tokenized with the same settings: a model belongs to one dictionary. A morpheme with fewer feature columns than the schema of the model reads is refused with an error; see Checking the dictionary.

With the head word and the function word

A model file holds the schema of its dictionary, which gives the head word and the function word of each bunsetsu. The following writes the result in the lattice format. The heads are a placeholder here, every bunsetsu depending on the next one; the parser finds them.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let schema = model.schema();
let count = ranges.len();
let bunsetsu = ranges
    .into_iter()
    .enumerate()
    .map(|(index, range)| {
        let positions = schema.positions(&morphemes[range.clone()]);
        let mut bunsetsu = Bunsetsu::new(range, (index + 1 < count).then_some(index + 1));
        bunsetsu.positions = positions;
        bunsetsu
    })
    .collect();
let sentence = Sentence::new(morphemes, bunsetsu)?;
let mut output = Vec::new();
lattice::write(&mut output, &sentence)?;
print!("{}", String::from_utf8(output)?);
}
* 0 1D 0/1
彼	名詞,代名詞,一般,*,*,*,彼,カレ,カレ
は	助詞,係助詞,*,*,*,*,は,ハ,ワ
* 1 2D 0/1
本	名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,本,ホン,ホン
を	助詞,格助詞,一般,*,*,*,を,ヲ,ヲ
* 2 -1D 0/1
読ん	動詞,自立,*,*,五段・マ行,連用タ接続,読む,ヨン,ヨン
だ	助動詞,*,*,*,特殊・タ,基本形,だ,ダ,ダ
。	記号,句点,*,*,*,*,。,。,。
EOS

Training a model

The model for IPADIC that Lindera releases has a chunker, and so have the models for UniDic. To train one of your own from training data:

cargo run --release -p lindera-dependency --features train -- train-chunker \
    --input train.lattice --output chunker.model

The model is for IPADIC unless --dictionary-name names another dictionary (unidic, unidic-cwj or unidic-csj): the name and the schema of that dictionary then go into the model, and the columns, the template and the coefficient are the ones for it.

On the train file of UD Japanese-GSD converted with IPADIC, this takes a few seconds and ends with:

train.lattice: 7024 sentences
iterations: 126
feature strings: 4325
weights: 8656
bytes: 261851

The output is a model file for the dictionary ipadic, with the chunker as its only part. Training the same data again gives the same bytes. The weights are f64. The format may change until the first release.

OptionDefaultMeaning
--regularizationl1l1 or l2
--lambda0.5The coefficient of the regularization
--columnssurface,pos,cformThe columns the template reads: surface, pos (the part of speech as its levels joined by -), ctype (conjugation type), cform (conjugation form), base (base form)
--templateThe template of CaboCha's chunker with five lines for a third columnA file in the format of CRF++
--max-iterations1000The largest number of iterations
--threadsThe number of CPUsThe number of threads

chunk segments the morphemes of a file again with a model, for evaluate to compare with the answer:

cargo run --release -p lindera-dependency --features train -- chunk \
    --model chunker.model --input dev.lattice --output output.lattice

It writes every bunsetsu as depending on the next one: it measures the chunker alone. parse --input-layer morphemes segments and parses.

Accuracy

With the defaults, trained on the train file of UD Japanese-GSD (commit c662dc9) with IPADIC:

FPrecisionRecallSentences with every bunsetsu right
UD Japanese-GSD dev96.8597.02% (4,009 / 4,132)96.67% (4,009 / 4,147)432 / 506
UD Japanese-GSD test96.9296.85% (4,373 / 4,515)96.98% (4,373 / 4,509)459 / 542
UD Japanese-PUD98.0498.05% (9,649 / 9,841)98.03% (9,649 / 9,843)885 / 994

The defaults were chosen by a 10-fold cross-validation on the train file. The conjugation form helps, the conjugation type does not, and L1 is better than L2 with a model about fifty times smaller. The tables of the cross-validation are in the README of the crate, and scripts/dependency runs them again.

With UniDic

train-chunker --dictionary-name unidic (or unidic-cwj, unidic-csj) trains with other settings than for IPADIC: four columns, the surface, the part of speech, the conjugation form and the base form, with Template::unidic(), and L1 regularization with the coefficient 0.25. TrainOptions::for_dictionary gives the settings of a dictionary. As for IPADIC, an option of the command replaces any of them.

The settings were chosen again by the cross-validation on the train file, with UniDic CWJ, and hold with the two other dictionaries. The base form of UniDic is the lexeme (語彙素), which is the same for the ways a word is written; it helps here, and it did not with IPADIC. F over the 10 folds, the sentences only one of the two settings segments right, and McNemar's test:

unidic-csj96.9497.0874 / 1310.0001

DictionaryUD Japanese-GSD devUD Japanese-GSD testUD Japanese-PUD
unidic96.89 and 97.03 (p 0.09)97.08 and 97.24 (p 0.82)98.02 and 98.00 (p 1.00)

How the features are made

The feature strings are made in two steps that can each be replaced:

  1. Columns. For each morpheme, the columns of the model are read through the schema: the surface, the part of speech, the conjugation form.
  2. Template. A template in the format of CRF++ expands the columns of the morpheme and of its neighbours into feature strings: U02:%x[0,0] is the first column of the morpheme itself, U11:%x[-1,1] the second column of the one before. A position outside the sentence gives _B-1, _B+1 and so on.

The decoder sees only the feature strings and the table of weights. Chunker::features makes the strings and Chunker::labels decodes them, so an extractor of your own can feed the same decoder.

Parsing

Parsing finds, for each bunsetsu of a sentence, the bunsetsu it depends on. The parser module does it the way CaboCha and J.DepP do: it goes through the bunsetsu from left to right with a stack (shift-reduce), and a classifier answers one question at a time.

Lindera releases the model for IPADIC and the models for UniDic. To make one of your own, train it from training data: it takes a few seconds.

Parsing with a model

A model file holds the chunker and the parser of a dictionary. With both, a sentence goes from morphemes to dependencies:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::io;

use lindera_dependency::lattice::{self, LatticeMorpheme};
use lindera_dependency::model::Model;
use lindera_dependency::Sentence;

let model = Model::new(std::fs::read("ipadic.model")?)?;
let chunker = model.chunker().expect("the file has a chunker");
let parser = model.parser().expect("the file has a parser");

// The morphemes of 彼は赤い花を見た。 as IPADIC gives them.
let morphemes = vec![
    LatticeMorpheme::new("彼", "名詞,代名詞,一般,*,*,*,彼,カレ,カレ"),
    LatticeMorpheme::new("は", "助詞,係助詞,*,*,*,*,は,ハ,ワ"),
    LatticeMorpheme::new("赤い", "形容詞,自立,*,*,形容詞・アウオ段,基本形,赤い,アカイ,アカイ"),
    LatticeMorpheme::new("花", "名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,花,ハナ,ハナ"),
    LatticeMorpheme::new("を", "助詞,格助詞,一般,*,*,*,を,ヲ,ヲ"),
    LatticeMorpheme::new("見", "動詞,自立,*,*,一段,連用形,見る,ミ,ミ"),
    LatticeMorpheme::new("た", "助動詞,*,*,*,特殊・タ,基本形,た,タ,タ"),
    LatticeMorpheme::new("。", "記号,句点,*,*,*,*,。,。,。"),
];
let ranges = chunker.chunk(&morphemes)?;
let bunsetsu = parser.parse(&morphemes, &ranges)?;

// The result is a sentence the lattice format can hold.
let sentence = Sentence::new(morphemes, bunsetsu)?;
lattice::write(&mut io::stdout(), &sentence)?;
}
* 0 3D 0/1 0.000000
彼	名詞,代名詞,一般,*,*,*,彼,カレ,カレ
は	助詞,係助詞,*,*,*,*,は,ハ,ワ
* 1 2D 0/0 0.704616
赤い	形容詞,自立,*,*,形容詞・アウオ段,基本形,赤い,アカイ,アカイ
* 2 3D 0/1 0.000000
花	名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,花,ハナ,ハナ
を	助詞,格助詞,一般,*,*,*,を,ヲ,ヲ
* 3 -1D 0/1 0.000000
見	動詞,自立,*,*,一段,連用形,見る,ミ,ミ
た	助動詞,*,*,*,特殊・タ,基本形,た,タ,タ
。	記号,句点,*,*,*,*,。,。,。
EOS

Each bunsetsu has its head, the positions of its head word and of its function word, and the score of the decision that attached it: above 0, and the larger the surer. Here 赤い depends on 花を with the score 0.70. The score is 0 for the root and for a bunsetsu attached to the root, since that decision is not asked. Model::analyze does the two steps in one call; for many sentences, take the chunker and the parser once, as above. Both take &self and serve several threads.

How a sentence is parsed

A decision is about two bunsetsu, the source and the target: does the source depend on the target?

  1. A stack holds the bunsetsu that have no head yet. It starts with the first bunsetsu.
  2. Each following bunsetsu is taken as the target, and the top of the stack as the source.
  3. While the classifier says that the source depends on the target, the source gets its head and leaves the stack, and the next one is looked at.
  4. A source that is refused stays on the stack, and the target goes on top of it.
  5. The last bunsetsu is the root: whatever is on the stack when it comes depends on it, and the classifier is not asked.

The result is the tree the reference parsers assume: every head is to the right of its bunsetsu, no two arcs cross, and the last bunsetsu is the root. The number of decisions is under twice the number of bunsetsu, so the time is linear in the length of the sentence. A sentence of one or two bunsetsu asks nothing.

For 彼は | 本を | 読んだと | 言う, where 本を depends on 読んだと and the other two on 言う:

StackTargetDecisionAnswer
彼は本を彼は → 本をNo: 本を goes on the stack
彼は, 本を読んだと本を → 読んだとYes: 本を leaves the stack
彼は読んだと彼は → 読んだとNo: 読んだと goes on the stack
彼は, 読んだと言うnot askedBoth depend on 言う

Using the parser

The parser of a model file is a Parser with the classifier of the file. A Parser can be made from its parts as well: the schema of the dictionary, a feature set and a classifier. This classifier is made by hand, with one weight: a bunsetsu that ends in を depends on the next one.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::io;

use lindera_dependency::lattice::{self, LatticeMorpheme};
use lindera_dependency::parser::{FeatureSet, LinearClassifier, Parser};
use lindera_dependency::{Schema, Sentence};

// SFS is the surface of the function word of the source, and DIST:1
// says that the target is the next bunsetsu.
let pairs = HashMap::from([(("SFS:を".to_string(), "DIST:1".to_string()), 2.0)]);
let classifier = LinearClassifier::new(-1.0, HashMap::new(), pairs)?;
let parser = Parser::new(Schema::ipadic(), FeatureSet::cabocha(), classifier);

// 彼は | 本を | 読んだと | 言う
let morphemes = vec![
    LatticeMorpheme::new("彼", "名詞,代名詞,一般,*,*,*,彼,カレ,カレ"),
    LatticeMorpheme::new("は", "助詞,係助詞,*,*,*,*,は,ハ,ワ"),
    LatticeMorpheme::new("本", "名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,本,ホン,ホン"),
    LatticeMorpheme::new("を", "助詞,格助詞,一般,*,*,*,を,ヲ,ヲ"),
    LatticeMorpheme::new("読ん", "動詞,自立,*,*,五段・マ行,連用タ接続,読む,ヨン,ヨン"),
    LatticeMorpheme::new("だ", "助動詞,*,*,*,特殊・タ,基本形,だ,ダ,ダ"),
    LatticeMorpheme::new("と", "助詞,格助詞,引用,*,*,*,と,ト,ト"),
    LatticeMorpheme::new("言う", "動詞,自立,*,*,五段・ワ行促音便,基本形,言う,イウ,イウ"),
];
let bunsetsu = parser.parse(&morphemes, &[0..2, 2..4, 4..7, 7..8])?;
for (index, one) in bunsetsu.iter().enumerate() {
    println!("{index} -> {:?}, score {:?}", one.head, one.score);
}

// The result is a sentence the lattice format can hold.
let sentence = Sentence::new(morphemes, bunsetsu)?;
lattice::write(&mut io::stdout(), &sentence)?;
}
0 -> Some(3), score Some(0.0)
1 -> Some(2), score Some(1.0)
2 -> Some(3), score Some(0.0)
3 -> None, score Some(0.0)
